title: China’s modernisation models
author: none@none.com (Syed Sardar Ali)
content:
PAKISTAN was the first Muslim country to recognise the People’s Republic of China (PRC), with the two countries establishing diplomatic ties on May 21, 1951. During the past 75 years, the relationship has blossomed into an “all-wea­ther strategic cooperative partnership.” During the 1950s and 1960s, despite being a member of Western security alliances, Pakistan helped Beij­ing break out of its international isolation. Islam­abad’s diplomatic mediation in the early 1970s helped in the historic rapprochement between China and the United States. Reciprocally, China has supported Pakistan economically, militarily, and diplomatically, providing unwavering support for its national sovereignty, territorial integrity, and socioeconomic stability.
The PRC was established as a single-party ideological state in the Marxist-Leninist tradition. Under the British legacy, Pakistan established a federal state and Westminster-style parliamentary democracy. These governance structures have led to divergence in the modernisation trajectories of the two countries, despite the adoption of similar reform policies.
Both China and Pakistan have attempted to resolve the issue of inequitable distribution of agricultural land. The Communist Party of China (CPC) solved the problem by distributing land titles to 300 million peasants using radical measures. Despite possessing less than 10 per cent of the world’s arable land, China produces about 25pc of global grain output. In Pakistan, landlords undermined all attempts at land reforms by falsifying records. Currently, 67pc rural households in Pakistan own no land. Despite having the world’s largest contiguous canal system, Pakistan is ranked 106 out of 123 countries in the Global Hunger Index.
The ideal of women’s emancipation has been pursued by both China and Pakistan. Starting with the Marriage Law of 1950, China has passed nearly 100 laws and regulations, including the landmark Law on the Protection of Rights and Interests of Women 1992. Today China, at 65pc, is ahead of the global average in female labour for­ce participation. Traditionally, family life in Pak­­istan has been ruled by feudal and tribal cust­o­­ms, colonial-era personal laws, and religious precepts. Pakistan promulgated the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 but conditions in rural areas remained unchanged. In the Global Gender Gap Index of the World Economic Forum, Pakis­t­­an ranks at the very bottom: 148 out of 148 countries.
In China, modernisation emerged as one of the central purposes of the state.
Soviet-style five-year plans have been used by both China and Pakistan. Since 1953, China has successfully completed 15 five-year plans. In the process it has been transformed from a subsistence agricultural economy into the largest manufacturing power, the biggest exporter, and the only country in history to achieve a trade surplus of one trillion dollars. Pakistan has implemented eight five-year plans but only the second plan (1960-65) succeeded in achieving its targets. Pakistan discontinued the practice in 1998. Slow growth in the last two decades has pushed Pakistan below its South Asian neighbours in per capita GDP. The country runs an annual trade deficit of around $30 billion and Pakistan has received more assistance packages from the International Monetary Fund than any other country.
Similar modernisation measures producing dissimilar outcomes is the result of differences in political ideology, structure of the state, and form of government of China and Pakistan.
From the British, Pakistan inherited the tradition of liberalism where the state exists primarily to protect individual rights and private property. It is not an instrument to achieve national goals. Socialism distinguishes between different modes of production and the state is an agent of progress. In China, modernisation emerged as one of the central purposes of the state and the supreme responsibility of the party. Political debates in Pakistan remain confined to changes of government. In Pakistan, modernisation never became the topic of political debate and state resources have never been marshalled to achieve it.
In China, the CPC solved the problem of lack of state institutions by building party network. Fusion of the party and the state meant that the party’s directives and policies were seamlessly translated into state legislation and administrative action. The party-state model has proved to be the perfect strategy for building modern bureaucracy. Pakistan inherited the colonial-era civil service but nepotism and patronage gradually eroded its essence of impersonality, specialisation, and merit. With every political government the capacity of the state declined, rendering it incapable of maintaining security, collecting taxes, and enforcing policies.
Pakistan adopted multiparty adult franchise democracy but the society had no tradition of resolution of differences through rational discourse, no common civic public good, and no equality. Inevitably, Pakistan’s democracy morphed into demagoguery and populism. The communists enshrined in the Chinese constitution the CPC’s leadership as a foundational pillar of the Chinese state. This allows the ruling party to focus on governance. While Pakistan’s political institutions have pushed the country ever deeper into crises, the combination of progressive ideology, appropriate state model, and correct governance system has allowed China to focus on the grand project of national rejuvenation.
For developing countries, the universal lesson is that modernisation is not possible without an effective state but not all state types are equal in their capacity. The Westphalian state model and universal-franchise democracy, when adopted by non-Western societies, do not necessarily result in a functional state and a stable government. To be effective, a state and its governance system must align with local conditions and be in harmony with society’s stage of evolution. Without an effective state machinery, even the most elaborate modernisation plans can neither foster sustainable development nor secure a happy and prosperous life for the people.
The writer has a background in public administration. He has worked with international financial institutions, including the World Bank.
Published in Dawn, November 14th, 2026

title: Derailed by design
author: none@none.com (Naeem Sadiq)
content:
PAKISTAN Railways has become synonymous with the image of a decaying organisation: accident-prone, loss-making and inefficient. Not many are willing to admit that mismanagement, unsteady wagons, rickety tracks and 18th-century mindset have reduced the Railways to a near-death existence. Even when it reluctantly continues to chug, rattle and rumble, everyone knows that it is managed and operated in a way not much different from a lorry adda across the road. The only option left seems to lie in the old Dakota Indian tribal wisdom: “When you discover that you are riding a dead horse, the best strategy is to dismount.”
Pakistan Railways has simply run out of steam. A meltdown was only natural. Managerially, technically and financially bankrupt, it finds it impossible to transport passengers and goods safely and efficiently. It is headed by a bureaucrat and a politician. While declaring a railway emergency, the only actions the minister in charge could think of were punishments received by schoolchildren. Come to work on Sundays, no leave for three months, send daily reports (homework) to the ministry and use trains for travelling on duty.
Even a novice would immediately figure out the pointlessness of these measures. A better informed and competent management would have suggested identifying root causes, taking actions to prevent their recurrence and verifying them for their effectiveness.
Imagine a railway in the year 2026 that cannot use even a basic email system for its routine internal and external communication (a disease proudly shared by the entire government of Pakistan.) Reportedly, an experimental email was recently sent to 40 senior officials of the Railways. Thirty-nine never responded, while one was responded to by a clerk saying that a reply was not possible due to the absence of the boss.
Pakistan Railways needs non-political & professional management.
Compare the sense of responsibility and ethics that differentiate Pakistan Railways from the rest of the world. Following the train derailment at Hatfield, UK on Oct 17, 2000, which killed four passengers, the Railtrack CEO Gerald Corbett took less than 24 hours to tender his resignation. Mohsen Aghaie, the head of the Iranian Railways was quick to resign after a train collision that killed 44 people in Iran in November 2016, describing his departure as a matter of social responsibility and sympathy for the survivors.
Pakistan Railways, on the other hand, met with 448 railway disasters between 2021 and 2025, leaving 169 dead and over 400 injured or crippled for life. Not a single Railways chairman even remotely contemplated a resignation. There is no record of any official above grade 19 ever having been held accountable. No wonder the lack of accountability has helped the Railways perfect the art of digging progressively deeper pits and incurring bigger losses each year. It incurred a financial loss of Rs47.49 billion in 2022, Rs48.2bn in 2023, Rs51.38bn in 2024 and Rs61.19bn in 2025. What crime have the people of Pakistan committed to carry such loss-making and life-extracting burden on their shoulders?
Track-related derailments, unmanned crossings and train collisions are the three most cited reasons for the repeated railway accidents. Pakistan Railways management has been negligent of not addressing these issues. A quick root cause analysis and effective corrective actions could have fixed these issues for good. Not equipped to either think or act on modern professional lines, it has finally come to an expected dead end.
Can a clueless bureaucratic structure that allows hu­­man waste to fall directly on railway tracks, from stationary and moving tra­ins, be entrus­t­­ed to underta­ke the task of running a Railways system?
Pakistan Ra-ilways needs to replace its current setup with a completely non-political, non-bureaucratic and professional management. It needs a world-class occupational health and safety system. It needs a proactive hazard identification and risk assessment programme to fix its fragile tracks, its 1,416 unmanned crossings, and its archaic communication system.
For all this, the Railways does not need billions of dollars. It needs billions of neurons. Every developed country’s railway has a system called Occupational Health and Safety Management System based on national or international standards such as ISO 45001.
Pakistan Railways appears to have no clue of any such system. Being an occupational health and safety engineer, may I humbly offer to spend two months (as an entirely pro bono activity) to help Pakistan Railways set up such a world-class safety management system.
The writer is an industrial engineer and a volunteer social activist.

title: Pakistan’s polio paradox
author: none@none.com (Fayyaz Ahmad Khan)
content:
PAKISTAN’S latest polio case, a seven-month-old boy in Khyber district reported on Nov 6, is the ninth of 2026 and the seventh in Khyber Pakh­tun­khwa. It is another reminder of how elusive eradication has proved. After three decades of campa­i­gns, billions of dollars of international support, a field force of more than 400,000 workers, and the creation of one of the largest polio programmes in the world, the country has still not eliminated a pre­­ventable disease. Pakistan has not turned its abi­­lity to run campaigns into a system of public health protection that families trust, and that failure, which lies behind much of the refusal, is why the virus survives.
The obstacles usually cited are real: insecurity, population movement, and difficult terrain keep teams from some children, while refusals, misinformation, and religious misconceptions keep others from being vaccinated. They do not account for the survival of the virus in communities that vaccination teams reach campaign after campaign and where families still turn the teams away. The reason lies beyond the vaccine, in the relationship between the state, its health institutions, and the communities they serve, and in whether those communities trust them.
Political scientist Bo Rothstein has argued that trust in government depends on the quality and im­­partiality of public institutions: people trust ins­­titutions they experience as fair and reliable. Com­munication alone does not build trust, and a nati­onal health priority cannot command it. It grows out of people’s everyday experience of the state.
The polio programme mobilises on a scale few public institutions in Pakistan can match. It deploys hundreds of thousands of vaccinators, maps households, monitors coverage, and returns repeatedly for the children who were missed. That capacity has saved many thousands of children from paralysis and remains essential to eradication. Beside that achievement stands the failure: the state’s ability to reach almost every household with polio drops has not become a working system of routine immunisation and basic healthcare.
For many families, particularly in underserved parts of the country, the polio team may be one of the few regular points of contact with the state. A vaccinator arrives at the doorstep, sometimes several times a year, to administer polio drops. The same household may have no functioning health facility within reach, no routine childhood vaccines, no maternal care, and no clean drinking water. The state is visible when it wants to vaccinate a child, and often invisible when that child or family needs anything else.
Pakistan’s polio programme has acknowledged that communities are using demand-based boycotts as a bargaining chip to draw attention to their problems.
The contrast is sharpest in southern KP, where communities have boycotted polio campaigns to press the government on demands that have gone unanswered for years. Misinformation and religious opposition explain few of these boycotts.
The British Medical Journal reported in December 2023 that tribal jirgas in southern KP had declared 677 boycotts during the year, with demands that ran from electricity, roads, and livelihoods to ref­u­­se collection. Pakistan’s own polio programme ack­nowledged that communities were using dem­and-based boycotts as a bargaining chip to draw attention to their problems. When a vaccination rou­­nd is the only occasion on which citizens can obtain ba­­sic services, the fault lies in the system of government as a whole. In some places a boycott is one of the few acts to which the government is compelled to respond, and communities have learnt as much.
The frontline has weaknesses of its own. Too few female vaccinators and frequent changes of team members, with thin training for all of them, spoil the encounter at the door. Vaccinators do not always explain convincingly why a child needs repeated doses, least of all to parents who believe that earlier campaigns should have been enough, and programmes make too little use of trusted local figures who understand the concerns of families. Even a better trained and more persuasive team, though, cannot make up for the absence of reliable public services.
Repeated visits can also do harm when families experience them as an imposition. For families who see little improvement in their lives, each arrival of a polio team can confirm that the state cares about one disease and one campaign, and little about the wellbeing of their children.
The response is to make vaccination part of a broader and more consistent public health presen­­ce, by strengthening routine immunisation and pri­­mary healthcare. The outreach capacity the pol­io programme has built should find the children rou­­tine immunisation has missed and connect their families with regular health services. That takes trained health workers, reliable vaccine supplies, accessible facilities, and continuity of care, well beyond the occasional catch-up activities atta­ched to polio campaigns, so that immunisation beco­mes a regular function of the district health system.
Behind this is the institutional separation between the polio programme and the wider health system. For years the National and Provincial Emergency Operations Centres have run as a well-funded parallel structure, answerable in large part to international donors, which mobilises large resources for campaign days while the provincial health departments beside them remain short of funds and bound by procedure. The dedicated funding, staffing, surveillance, and management arrangements that let the polio programme operate at scale belong inside the permanent health infrastructure of the provinces.
Communities also need channels for their wider concerns, through local administration and elected representatives, and those channels have to work independently of vaccination campaigns. Otherwise the government teaches communities that withholding children from vaccination is an effective way to secure electricity, water, or roads.
The responsibility rests with the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination, with the provincial governments, above all in KP, and with international donors, who should measure success by the strength of district health services as well as by the number of children reached in each round. Eradication depends on the campaigns, with better trained and more representative teams, and on what the campaigns cannot supply: a health system that protects children between rounds.
When a vaccination team arrives at a door, the family should see it as part of a state that also protects their children and listens to them. Until that is so, Pakistan may go on running polio campaigns, and the conditions that make eradication so difficult will stay as they are.
The writer is a strategic communication and public health professional, with experience across Asia, Africa and the Middle East.

title: Mineral wealth
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S mineral wealth offers an opportunity to attract investment, earn foreign exchange and support long-term economic growth. But turning this potential into reality will require more than promises. At the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026, Deputy PM Ishaq Dar has promised predictable policies and institutional support to investors interested in the country’s mineral resources. Such assurances are welcome. However, investors will need more than that. The country’s experience with large mining projects has not always inspired confidence. The Reko Diq dispute remains an important reminder of what can happen when agreements and government commitments become contentious. We cannot afford another dispute that damages the country’s credibility. Policy consistency must therefore extend beyond individual governments. That said, mining rights must be awarded through transparent processes, with clear contractual obligations and effective regulatory oversight.
Moreover, mineral development must benefit local populations. Communities should receive their share of employment, as well as better public services and improved infrastructure. Without local support, even commercially viable projects can falter. Additionally, Islamabad must avoid becoming merely a supplier of raw materials to the world. Exporting unprocessed minerals will bring some foreign exchange, but it will not deliver wider economic gains. The real opportunity lies in transfer of technology for refining minerals and producing finished goods locally. This would require investment in processing facilities and related industries. The aim must be to build an industrial base around mineral resources rather than simply dig them out and ship them abroad. The state should also resist the temptation to present minerals as a solution to Pakistan’s long-term economic difficulties. They can contribute significantly to sustainable growth and help diversify exports. But no country has ever developed on mineral wealth or exports alone. Natural resources can provide capital for development, but they cannot replace the hard work of building productive industries. Mineral wealth must become part of a wider industrialisation strategy. The country needs to raise productivity across manufacturing and agriculture, and develop products that can find markets abroad.

title: Constrained partnership
author: none@none.com (Zafar Mirza)
content:
“Trust takes years to build, seconds to break, and forever to repair.”
Anonymous
THIS observation aptly describes Pakistan’s relationship with one of its most important international health partners.
Since 2003, the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tu­­berculosis and Malaria has disbursed more than $1.1 billion to Pakistan’s HIV, tuberculosis and malaria programmes. In August 2020, however, it invoked its Additional Safeguard Policy (ASP) on Pakistan.
Behind this bureaucratic terminology lies an extraordinary decision: the Global Fund no longer had sufficient confidence in the country’s arrangements for managing its gra­nts and implementing disease-control programmes.
More than six years later, this decision deserves serious public scrutiny.
    
Established in 2002, the Global Fund is one of the most successful innovations in international health financing. It mobilises resources to support countries fighting these three diseases and has helped save an estimated 72 million lives globally. Pakistan has been a significant beneficiary.
The Global Fund normally operates through a partnership model in which national stakeholders identify priorities, nominate implementing organisations and oversee grants through a Country Coordinating Mechanism (CCM). The underlying philosophy is country ownership: international resources should strengthen national institutions, not substitute for them.
The Global Fund’s observations point to serious weaknesses in governance & institutional accountability.
In 2004, the Global Fund Board adopted ASP to address situations where normal funding arrangements could not adequately protect its investments. It permits oversight and direct involvement in selecting principal recipients and implementing partners. In effect, decisions normally taken by national institutions can be assumed by the international financing agency.
This is an exceptional, temporary arrangement, reflecting serious concerns about governance, institutional capacity, accountability or programme implementation. Since its introduction, it has been invoked in around 30 countries but revoked in only three: Cuba, Myanmar and Côte d’Ivoire. This shows that entering ASP is easier than exiting it.
Why was Pakistan placed under ASP? The ans­wer lies in a candid letter dated Aug 6, 2020, from the Global Fund to the Pakistan government.
It expressed serious dissatisfaction with Pakistan’s response to HIV and TB, noting stagnating or declining TB notifications and an almost unchecked increase in HIV incidence. Significantly, it stated that public-sector principal recipients had failed to translate domestic and external financing into effective programmes.
The letter specifically criticised the performance of the Common Management Unit (CMU), responsible for coordinating the three disease programmes, and identified inadequate leadership in managing challenges arising from devolution.
These observations point to serious weaknesses in governance, leadership, coordination and institutional accountability. Consider this: Between 2020 and 2022, Pakistan changed the national coordinator of the CMU 10 times in three years. Many appointments were political.
The epidemiological consequences are equally troubling. While many states have reduced new HIV infections, Pakistan has moved in the opposite direction. According to WHO and UNAIDS estimates reported in Dec 2025, annual new infections increased from approximately 16,000 in 2010 to 48,000 in 2024 — a 200pc increase.
ASP’s implications extend beyond these programmes. For a country seeking international inv­estment, development assistance and credibility in global institutions, its inability to demonstrate satisfactory governance of externally financed hea­­lth programmes sends a deeply damaging message.
But ASP should not be viewed merely as an international embarrassment. Its more serious implication is the erosion of national ownership. When external partners increasingly determine arrangements, domestic institutions risk becoming less accountable for results.
Pakistan must therefore develop a credible, time-bound roadmap for exiting ASP.
The Aug 2020 letter identified the conditions for its revocation: timely provincial budget disbursements for HIV and TB; satisfactory programme performance and financial risk management; demonstrated political commitment; compliance with audit recommendations, etc.
These are not unreasonable demands.
Federal and provincial governments must jointly establish a high-level mechanism to monitor progress against each condition through independently verifiable indicators.
Civil society and affected communities must also be meaningfully engaged.
There is another dimension requiring urgent attention: financial sustainability.
For over two decades, Pakistan has depended heavily on the Global Fund for essential components of its HIV, TB and malaria responses. In 2024, 90pc of HIV financing came from the Fund. This assistance has been invaluable. But indefinite dependence on external financing is neither desirable nor realistic, particularly as international development assistance comes under increasing pressure.
Pakistan needs a carefully planned transition towards greater domestic financial responsibility. This does not mean abruptly replacing Global Fund resources or imposing unaffordable obligations on provincial governments overnight.
    
The FCDO-financed, Oxford Policy Managem­e­nt-implemented Global Fund Accelerator Prog­ra­mme is providing valuable analytical support and recommendations. Federal and provincial governments must make optimal use of this opportunity.
They should negotiate a gradual increase in domestic financing. Public financing should progressively assume responsibility for recurrent expenditures, while increasingly covering medicines and prevention services.
Crucially, exiting ASP and transitioning from donor dependence are related but distinct processes.
The Global Fund has stood by Pakistan through successive health emergencies and institutional challenges. Its continued engagement, even after invoking ASP, demonstrates that its objective is not to abandon Pakistan but to protect investments and improve results. Pakistan must respond with the seriousness this partnership deserves.
Ultimately, the most compelling argument for reform is not the restoration of international prestige. It is the right of millions of Pakistanis to effective prevention, diagnosis and treatment. The real achievement will be transforming a constrained partnership into a confident, accountable and genuinely country-owned response to three preventable and treatable diseases.
The writer is a former health minister, adjunct professor of health systems and population health, president of Pakistan Association of Lifestyle Medicine and convener of Lok Sehat.
Published in Dawn, November 13th, 2026

title: Ambition without scale?
author: none@none.com (Ehsan Malik)
content:
PAKISTAN’S newly announced Auto Policy 2026-31 promises cheaper vehicles, higher localisation, exports, employment, improved safety and cleaner transportation. These are worthy objectives. But can they be achieved simultaneously in an industry constrained by limited scale, proliferating makes and models, and the absence of competitive upstream steel, petrochemical and aluminium industries?
More importantly, does the policy risk undermining one of the few enduring achievements of decades of automotive protection: the engineering capabilities developed by component manufacturers, with applications in agriculture, defence and other industries?
The policy deserves credit for recognising that protection has not delivered internationally competitive vehicles. Gradual tariff reductions, export targets and electric-vehicle incentives signal change. But reducing tariffs without addressing high energy, taxation and financing costs risks weakening domestic manufacturers before they become competitive.
    
Previous auto policies have produced an insufficiently recognised benefit: the engineering capabilities developed by component manufacturers. Guided by international assemblers, Pakistani firms have acquired expertise in precision machining, sheet-metal pressing, plastic moulding, rubber products, glass, wiring and numerous other components. Industrial clusters around Port Qasim, Lahore-Sheikhupura and elsewhere demonstrate capabilities extending beyond automobiles. Losing them would erode an industrial foundation that Pakistan needs for manufacturing diversification and import substitution.
Competition among brands is desirable, but proliferation of incompatible platforms undermines supplier competitiveness.
Support for technological upgrading, testing and certification is welcome. However, indiscriminate tariff reductions could expose these firms to overseas competitors operating at vastly greater scale, before domestic cost disadvantages are addressed.
Protection should neither be indefinite nor un­­conditional. A differentiated, time-bound appro­ach should preserve engineering capabilities with demonstrable competitive potential, linking support to productivity, quality, scale and exports.
Mandatory localisation targets require scruti­ny. Components manufactured locally using im­­por­ted steel, polymers, machinery and tooling cannot reasonably be counted as entirely indigenous. Pakistan lacks integrated automotive-grade steel, petrochemical and aluminium supply chains. The appropriate measure is domestic value addition after deducting imported inputs, including those embedded in locally purchased components.
Higher local procurement does not necessarily deliver equivalent foreign-exchange savings. Policy must measure genuine indigenous value addition, technological upgrading and net foreign-exchange contribution separately.
Pakistan’s limited vehicle market is increasingly divided among manufacturers, models and variants. Each additional platform can require separate moulds, dies and tooling. Small production runs raise costs and discourage sophisticated manufacturing.
Competition among brands is desirable, but proliferation of incompatible platforms undermines supplier competitiveness. Common components, platform sharing, contract manufacturing and supplier consolidation should be encouraged.
Pakistan’s motorcycle industry offers an instructive parallel. Standardised designs, large volumes, extensive vendor networks and a substantial replacement market have enabled component manufacturers to develop capabilities while making transportation accessible to millions.
Cars require more demanding standards and higher tooling investment, but the lessons of affordability, standardisation and scale remain relevant.
Pakistan should encourage one or more safe, fuel-efficient, affordable small-car platforms through collaboration with established international manufacturers. Shared components and higher volumes could support meaningful domestic value addition, strengthen vendors and eventually create export opportunities.
Encouraging electric vehicles is appropriate, particularly motorcycles, three-wheelers, small cars and public transport. However, concessional imports of completely built-up vehicles and completely knocked-down kits may accelerate adoption without developing domestic engineering capabilities. The transition should include a roadmap enabling existing component manufacturers to enter EV supply chains.
The policy envisages approximately $6 billion in cumulative automotive exports over five years. But who will buy these vehicles?
Complete-vehicle exports depend on foreign principals allocating production and overseas markets to Pakistani operations. Such decisions are scale-dependent and cannot be mandated. Potential African and other markets present additional challenges. Pakistan generally lacks preferential trade agreements with these destinations, leaving its vehicles exposed to tariffs while competing against established Asian manufacturers.
Export incentives introduce another risk. WTO rules restrict subsidies contingent on export performance, while importing countries can impose countervailing duties following investigations establishing subsidisation and injury.
    
Export targets need identifiable customers, commercial commitments, market access and demonstrated net foreign-exchange earnings.
The proposed Automotive Development Levy, expected to raise Rs232bn over five years, raises another question. Pakistan’s experience with the Export Development Fund offers a cautionary lesson. Financed through a levy on exports, it supported various initiatives, but its effectiveness in delivering sustained competitiveness remains debatable. The government’s subsequent decision to review its utilisation, audit its accounts and abolish the surcharge raises legitimate questions about establishing another dedicated levy.
Public funding for shared testing facilities, technology transfer and skills development has merit. But taxing consumers to subsidise exports that remain uncompetitive risks replacing tariff protection with another permanent support mechanism.
Ultimately, Pakistan must distinguish between assembling vehicles, manufacturing competitive components and providing affordable mobility. These are related but different objectives.
The writer is a former CEO of Unilever Pakistan and the Pakistan Business Council.
Published in Dawn, November 13th, 2026

title: Climate challenges
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE poisonous smog blanketing Punjab is an immediate threat to public health, but it also points to a larger environmental crisis that Pakistan can no longer address through piecemeal measures. Lahore’s air quality index stood at a hazardous 358 on Wednesday, while other cities struggled under the same toxic haze.
Punjab’s government says better monitoring and enforcement have brought improvements over previous years. That is welcome, but the air remains dangerous. While pollution from India compounds the problem, Pakistan must also confront domestic emissions.
Moreover, smog is not the country’s only warning. Our climate crises are deeply interconnected. Repeated floods, punishing heatwaves and mounting water stress show how exposed Pakistan is to climate shocks, and how urgently it needs lasting solutions.
    
At COP31, PM Shehbaz Sharif outlined a cleaner energy future that deserves support. He pointed to nearly 22 gigawatts of rooftop solar capacity added in two years, much of it driven by households seeking relief from expensive electricity.
Pakistan has backed a pledge to increase electricity’s share of energy use to 35pc by 2035 and aims for electric vehicles to account for 30pc of new vehicle sales by 2030. These shifts could help reduce fossil-fuel dependence and, especially through cleaner transport, cut harmful emissions. But an energy transition is not, by itself, a climate policy.
    
Pakistan also needs to protect communities from floods and extreme heat, safeguard water supplies and adapt agriculture to changing conditions. The PM rightly called for concessional finance and affordable technology. Rich industrialised countries bear much of the responsibility for global warming and must help vulnerable nations cope. Yet appeals for international climate justice must run alongside serious action at home.
That action requires more than ambitious targets or seasonal restrictions. Authorities must enforce vehicle and industrial emission standards, expand public transport, support farmers in ending crop burning and make clean technology accessible beyond affluent households. Cities must be better prepared for floods and extreme weather, while rural communities need help coping with rising temperatures and water shortages.
Federal and provincial governments must work together and ensure that environmental regulations are properly enforced. Businesses, too, must reduce their environmental impact, while citizens have a responsibility to conserve resources, avoid polluting their surroundings and demand action from the state.
None of this will be easy in a country facing serious fiscal constraints. But the cost of delay is already being paid in illness, damaged livelihoods and repeated disruption. Pakistan cannot afford to confront its climate crises one disaster, one season and one international summit at a time.
Published in Dawn, November 13th, 2026

title: Beyond diplomacy
author: none@none.com (Laraib Sajid)
content:
PAKISTAN’S relationship with competing global powers, and effective participat­i­­­on in international peace efforts, have of­­fe­red the country avenues to exercise inf­­luence beyond its economic weight. It has managed to grab international attention due to its role as a mediator in facilitating dialogue between the United States and Iran.
However, diplomatic recognition does not automatically translate into economic prosperity for a country. Pakistan needs to convert its growing diplomatic relevance into sustainable and durable economic partnerships, which include foreign direct investment, regional connectivity and technology transfer.
Pakistan has increasingly sought to use international platforms to seek its economic interests. Its engagements with multilateral forums such as the United Nations, OIC and SCO provide opportunities to promote trade, attract investment and build partnerships. The economic diplomacy initiatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its dedicated coordination with the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC) highlight an acknowledgement that economic policy and foreign policy can no longer operate in isolation.
Last month, the SIFC presented an inv­e­­stment pipeline to a Senate committee comprising 38 projects with an anticipated in­­v­estment potential of approximately $40 bil­­lion. This is an encouraging indicator of opportunities being pursued. However, this investment pipeline should not be conside­red the same as realised investment. Inves­­tors assess the legal, regulatory and administrative environment in which their inv­­estments will operate instead of merely relying on the strength of diplomatic assurances.
Constitutional federalism needs to work for economic development.
The problem does not simply lie in burea­ucratic inefficiency; rather it goes deep into the unresolved question of Pakistan’s fede­ral structure. The 18th Amendment stren­g­thened provincial autonomy by transferring responsibilities from the centre to the provinces. Some of the sectors in which SIFC at­­tracts investments including tourism, agriculture, and minerals require provincial participation as they are outside the mandate of the Federal Legislative List. There­fore, an investment proposal initiated at the federal level may still require provincial approvals and administrative permissions.
The SIFC was formulated in 2023 through an amendment in the Board of Investment Ordinance, 2001. However, it is unable to resolve the institutional divide between the centre and provinces on matters related to investment. Section 10E of the Ordinance empowers SIFC to issue recommendations, advice or directions to federal regulatory bodies, public sector entities, authorities and government depart­­ments. This section does not expressly extend this directive authority to provincial governments.
Such hurdles create an uncomfortable situation for international investors. An in­­v­­estor attracted through assurance of a st­reamlined approval process and diplom­atic engagements may encounter delays once the project reaches the provincial level.
The solution does not lie in undermining provincial autonomy or doing expansive interpretation of SIFC’s mandate. Such a solution may give rise to constitutional disputes and alienate provincial governments. The goal should be to make the existing constitutional federalism work for economic development.
There are institutional mechanisms that can bridge the divide. The Interprovincial Coordination Committee provides a mechanism for coordination between the federation and provinces. Its mandate includes promoting a uniform approach to matters of common national concern. Investment-related bottlenecks can be for­mally placed be­­­fore it. The Ministry of Inter-Provincial Coordination must transition from its mostly reactive position to an active facilitator of investment-related coordination if this system is to be successful.
Another option is provided by the Provincial Investment Committees established under Section 15 of the BOI Ordinance. These committees are meant to support the BOI, promote investment within provinces, and ensure ongoing cooperation with it. They may function as SIFC’s provincial counterparts if properly constituted and operationalised.
The Council of Common Interests should continue to be accessible for issues coming under its constitutional purview. It is important, however, to distinguish between ordinary administrative cooperation needed to handle individual investment projects and high-level constitutional and policy disagreements.
Ultimately, Pakistan’s diplomatic outreach must be matched by institutional credibility at home. Pakistan cannot ask international investors to place confidence in its economic future while leaving unresolved the question of how its own government will work together to secure that future.
The writer is a lawyer based in Islamabad.
Published in Dawn, November 13th, 2026

title: Midterm lessons
author: none@none.com (Asif Saad)
content:
THERE will be many explanations for the outcome of the US midterm elections. Some will focus on the Iran war, personalities, inflation, tariffs or the divide between Republicans and Democrats.
The explanation that interests me most is more fundamental.
The US economy was hardly in collapse. The stock market had recently reached unp­recedented highs, economic growth remai­n­­ed respectable, unemployment was not a ma­­jor concern, and overall household weal­­th had reached high levels by mid-2026.
Yet consumer sentiment remained close to record lows, and economic pressure and the cost of living were among the strongest motivations in the election.
Growth is no longer enough as a political argument.
There is an important message in that contrast. An economy can generate great wealth without large numbers of people feeling that they are becoming better off.
This does not mean American voters have rejected capitalism. But it may represent another challenge to an idea that has influenced economic policy for decades; create favourable conditions for business, and the benefits will eventually spread through investment, jobs and higher incomes.
We call this trickle-down economics.
There is logic behind part of it. Businesses must make profits. Profitable companies can invest and create employment. What I question is the assumption that business prosperity will automatically become broader prosperity.
It may. But it does not have to. Profits can finance new factories and jobs. Technology can raise productivity without producing equivalent growth in employment.
This helps explain the apparent contradiction in the US. The stock market can create vast amounts of wealth for those who own financial assets while a worker whose inco­­me depends primarily on wages struggles.
Many citizens may ask very different qu­­estions; am I becoming more economically secure? Can my income keep pace with the cost of living? When enough people become doubtful about those answers, growth begins to lose its political legitimacy.
And this is where democracy enters the story.
Markets can allocate capital, determine prices and reward economic activity. They cannot decide whether the resulting distribution of wealth, opportunity and security remains acceptable to society.
Democracy provides that feedback. When people conclude that the economic bargain no longer works for them, elections provide a peaceful mechanism through which they can demand change.
That is the lesson Pakistan should pay attention to. We spend a great deal of time discussing economic stabilisation and growth. Forex reserves improve. Inflation falls. The current account looks better. The stock market rises.
All these matter. No economy can prosper for long without macroeconomic stability. But stabilisation and growth are not prosperity.
Pakistan has repeatedly gone through cycles in which macroeconomic stabilisation is achieved through adjustment of higher taxes, energy prices, reduced subsidies, tighter spending and slower demand.
Some of these measures may be unavoidable. But adjustment is never neutral. Higher taxes reduce disposable income and higher energy prices raise household and business costs. Subsidy cuts hurt those who relied on them, and tighter spending can weaken demand and employment.
A society can tolerate considerable inequality and difficult adjustment if people continue to believe that opportunity is open, and the system offers a route towards greater security.
It becomes harder when growth appears to occur somewhere else, for somebody else. The lesson from the US midterms is not that ca­­pitalism has been re­­jected. It is that growth is no longer enough as a political argument.
The US economy showed that it is possible to have strong gro­wth, low unemploym­ent and extra­­ordi­na­ry levels of financial wealth and still have voters deeply dissatisfied with their economic circumstances. Pakistan should take that ser­­iously. Macroeconomic stability is necessary.
But Pakistan should be conscious of the timing of the economic model it is now pursuing. Privatisation, deregulation, reducing the state’s commercial footprint and relying more on private enterprise are central to the reform programme.
But these are also elements of the market-led economic model that has dominated much of the West for several decades and whose outcomes are now being questioned by voters there. The lesson is not that Pakistan should reject markets. It is that we should not assume that markets, privatisation and growth will by themselves produce broadly shared prosperity.
None of them is sufficient if ordinary citizens cannot see a meaningful connection between national economic progress and their own lives. And in a real democracy, eventually they will say so.
The writer advises boards and CEOs on strategy, leadership and organisational transformation.

title: Used car imports
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE government’s effort to restrict used car imports appears to be faltering. So suggest the numbers. Despite tighter conditions and the abolition of the personal baggage scheme, used vehicles continue to enter the country in growing numbers through the gift scheme. More than 2,000 vehicles reportedly arrived in October alone. The figures suggest that restrictions have failed to stop the misuse of facilities meant for overseas Pakistanis. Imports of completely built-up (CBU) vehicles, including new and used cars, increased 40pc to $126m in the first quarter of this fiscal. This comes as the country struggles to contain its import bill and rebuild forex reserves. Every additional dollar spent on imported used cars adds to pressure on the external account. The concern is greater when such imports serve commercial interests rather than genuine national needs.
There are also serious questions about tax collection. Besides, payments are made through informal channels, while domestic sales take place largely in cash. It means that the government is losing revenue through undeclared transactions. The bigger concern is the damage to the domestic auto parts industry employing hundreds of thousands of workers directly and indirectly. When imported vehicles replace locally assembled ones, demand for these parts falls. The resulting loss of business threatens investment, employment and the progress made towards localisation. The new auto policy adds to those concerns by making imported CBU vehicles and parts cheaper. Assemblers may find it easier to source components from foreign suppliers rather than invest in local manufacturing. This would weaken an industry that has spent years building production capacity. There is a legitimate case for greater competition in the automobile market. Buyers deserve better quality and more affordable vehicles. Protecting an inefficient industry is not sustainable. But neither is encouraging imports that drain foreign exchange, weaken tax collection, put domestic jobs at risk, and turn the country into a junkyard.
Published in Dawn, November 13th, 2026

title: External sector turning points
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
THE slight increase in workers’ remittances reported for October prompted a host of questions directed to me. Here are the responses.
The rise is too small to matter. In fact, it falls far short of what it needs to be to serve its purpose: helping plug the trade deficit. There is no reason in the world for celebration based on one data outturn. What matters is the trend that a series of data points describe; most often, that trend is intelligible only when seen in its proper context.
So what is the proper context for remittances? First, remittances are traditionally how Pakis­tan’s economy finances its trade deficits. The trend is cyclical and reveals itself when you take a 12-month average of the total trade balance plus remittances, then plot that on a month-to-month basis. You will notice something. A wavy line emerges. From a low point in 2015, it rises slowly until it briefly turns positive — around $40 million — in November 2015. Then it plunges back below the X-axis, before bottoming out in July 2018 at around negative $1.45 billion.
This is trade balance plus remittances, mind you, so a negative value means remittances can’t plug the trade deficit, and the balance is being financed from reserves or borrowing. If you don’t see the reserves plunging by the same amount in that month, then you can be sure the balance is being financed by new borrowing, and that data will show up in the balance-of-payments whenever the next release comes along.
    
From July 2018, the line rises sharply again until it hits a fresh peak in November 2020 at around $100m. It then plunges again until it hits its second trough in July 2022 at negative $1.14bn. This is when another attempt to stabilise Pakistan’s economy by choking its imports began — abortively, as it turned out.
At least since June, the trade deficit’s growth has outstripped remittances.
After that, the next peak — $780m — was in March 2025; it has stayed above the X-axis for the most part, barring one or two months. But if the trend so far is anything to go by, the line has been falling since March, reaching $480m by September. This is the 12-month average. For September alone, the figure is closer to $150m. The October trade data has not yet been released, so we don’t know where the figure will be for that month. But given the pace of increase in imports, and the relative stagnation of export growth, grounds for excess optimism are conspicuous by their absence.
This is entirely in sync with the long-run trend of how Pakistan’s external sector behaves. It heaves and ebbs in cycles. Take the earliest low point of the trade deficit in some month and trace it forward. What you see is the trade deficit growing as imports outstrip exports each month, but remittances cover the gap. Hence, the overall current account in the balance of payments remains above zero. Then the trade deficit starts to grow beyond the ability of the remittances to cover. The current account falls into deficit. Borrowing increases during these months to cover the deficit.
As the required pace of borrowing increases, the government is unable to fetch dollars in quantities sufficient to pay for the deficit, and the reserves start to fall. Once that fall begins, it becomes very difficult to contain the situation. Eventually, the reserves drop to a level that necessitates a return to the IMF for a bailout. That bailout requires taking steps to choke imports and kill the fiscal deficit as well, and eventually normalcy returns, but at the cost of choking economic activity in the country.
    
Take four indicators and plot them from 2014 onwards (you can start earlier if you like). Plot exports, imports, remittances, and external payment obligations over a 12-month period from that year onward. For external obligations, use the total figure for “predetermined drains” given in the International Liquidity sheet released every month by the State Bank. What you’ll see is that exports are the slowest to grow over the years, while external obligations are the fastest. Here is what the numbers look like: exports have grown by 1.4x since 2014, imports by 1.6x, remittances by 2.7x, and external obligations by 4.6x.
This is the real long-run trend that needs to break before any indicator can mean anything. This year alone, for example, the trade deficit has grown faster than remittances. There are a few different ways to measure this growth, and each gives you slightly different numbers. But all of them show that, at least since June, the trade deficit’s growth has outstripped remittances. If this trend continues, then it shows we have already passed the peak that historically defines the turning point from growth to bust.
And there is little reason today to believe that the trend will turn around on its own. In past periods, governments had a story to tell at this point, even if the story held little water. In both past peaks, when the trade deficit began yawning and eating up all current inflows, both governments in power at each peak said their period had seen a large inflow of machinery that, once installed, would lead to export growth and reverse the trend.
That story failed to pan out both times. But at least it was there. What is the story now? What is this government’s plan for containing the trade deficit, which is only a few months away from outstripping remittances’ ability to plug it? The only story they’re running with these days is some urgency to see dramatic improvements in the country’s credit rating by June 2027. What is that in preparation for? More borrowing? If so, then welcome to the old world.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

title: Forex crowding out
author: none@none.com (Farooq Arby)
content:
THE State Bank of Pakistan (SBP)has successfully rebuilt foreign exchange reserves over the last three years. Much of this success, however, has been purchased by drawing liquidity directly out of the forex market. It attributes its purchases to improved market liquidity and describes their purpose as strengthening external buffers and the capacity to meet external obligations. These are legitimate considerations. Yet the extent to which dollars have been siphoned from the market to accumulate reserves raises concerns for the wider economy.
When the central bank becomes a persistent and dominant buyer of dollars in the market, it effectively crowds out some private businesses, which must compete with an institution that enjoys an informational advantage. While Pakistan is familiar with the crowding out of the private sector through large and persistent government borrowing to finance budget deficits, crowding out in the foreign exchange market is unprecedented.
If the forex market has sufficient depth, it can smoothly accommodate both the central bank’s purchases and the private sector’s requirements. But where the market is constrained, the adjustment has to take place somewhere. It may appear in the exchange rate, transaction spreads, delays in opening letters of credit (LCs), or restrictions on access to foreign currency. In effect, private sector buyers are either priced out of the market or pushed into waiting queues.
There have been several media reports of import payment delays and dollar rationing by some banks. Concerns about these practices have also surfaced in official trade assessments. The US National Trade Estimate Report 2026, for instance, records stakeholder concerns about delays in banks’ issuance of LCs, reportedly resulting from informal SBP limitations on commercial banks’ borrowing of foreign currency through the interbank market. The report also highlights that corporations and foreign equity holders have encountered administrative delays, documentation hurdles, and informal queuing systems when seeking to repatriate their profits, dividends, and royalties in dollars.
The SBP must reassess its market interventions.
Such restrictions carry consequences. Central banking, in essence, is not an accounting exercise and balance sheet management. Every action has microeconomic and macroeconomic repercussions for resource allocation, business costs, investment decisions, and, ultimately, economic growth. Thus, a policy intended to strengthen the country’s external position can, paradoxically, undermine investors’ sentiments and the productive capacity to generate future foreign exchange.
A further paradox concerns the exchange rate signal. Despite extensive purchases, the exchange rate is not responding. Conventional macroeconomic models offer limited help in explaining such interventions. Instead, an exchange rate microstructure approach, built on order flow, may offer a better explanation of exchange rate determination. Order flow refers to the buying and selling pressure generated by market participants. This approach recognises the importance of participants’ identities, information and trading behaviour in influencing exchange rate movements. A study by Evans and Lyons, published in the Journal of Political Economy in 2002, shows that order flow has substantial explanatory power for exchange rate changes.
When a central bank, which also issues licences to the market participants, enters the market, its order flow may convey its preferences about price as well as quantity. Forex dealers, observing this institutional order flow, may adjust their quotes and inventory positi­ons accordingly. Consequently, the exchange rate may increasingly reflect the central bank’s institutional prefere­nces rather than the underlying balance of forex demand and supply.
Granular level data can explain forex dynamics on the basis of the order flow model. The SBP has both the technical capacity and the high-frequency data required for such analysis. It could examine import payment delays, outstanding foreign exchange requests, transaction spreads, interbank turnover, and the daily pattern of its own purchases. A range of forex market data is already covered by IMF monitoring and reporting requirements on a daily basis. Greater transparency and wider dissemination of this data may also allow independent researchers to apply an order flow model to exchange rate formation in Pakistan.
Reserve accumulation is a necessary but not sufficient condition for stability, which ultimately depends on the economy’s ability to generate foreign exchange through exports, investment, and productive activity. The SBP must, therefore, assess its market interventions within a robust analytical framework and develop an exit strategy for its dollar purchases for reserve accumulation.
The writer is an economist.

title: Unspent funds
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE slow pace of development spending shows how public investment continues to bear the brunt of efforts to create a primary fiscal surplus, while wasteful government expenditure remains largely protected. The numbers speak for themselves. The government spent just 10.4pc of the Rs1tr PSDP allocation during the first four months of the current year. Even against the Rs412.3bn authorised for spending, actual utilisation remained exceptionally low. Several ministries could not spend even a single rupee. This pattern is hardly new. Successive governments have routinely sacrificed development spending to meet fiscal targets, particularly under IMF programmes. The lender’s strict conditions on fiscal deficits and primary balances leave little room for development works. They find it easier to delay development than to confront politically influential lobbies, reduce administrative waste, or cut their own privileges. Public investment becomes the easiest adjustment whenever revenues fall short.
The current figures, however, should not be mistaken for the final spending position. Disbursements are likely to accelerate as the fiscal year progresses, particularly towards its closing months. Such hurried spending reflects poor planning and weak project preparation. Governments announce ambitious development allocations for political reasons without ensuring that projects are ready for implementation. The result is a rush to spend towards the end of the year, often at the expense of quality and value for money. The underlying problem is equally clear. The government has failed to broaden the tax base and raise the tax-to-GDP ratio, which has for long hovered around 10pc or lower. Without a stronger revenue base, there is little money available for development. The burden of financing the state continues to fall on a relatively narrow segment of taxpayers, while large sections of the economy remain outside the tax net. A fiscal surplus has little meaning if it is achieved by starving the economy of investment. Public infrastructure is essential for raising productivity and improving living standards. Its neglect creates higher costs for future generations. The government must raise more revenue by broadening the tax net. It must also examine its own non-development expenditure and cut wasteful spending. The country needs a revenue system capable of financing growth, not one that repeatedly makes investment its first casualty.

title: The unmaking of…
author: none@none.com (F.S. Aijazuddin)
content:
AMERICAN WASPs have lost their sting. The recent US midterm elections results are balm to the pain felt after Donald Trump’s return to the White House two years ago.
This November, that surge of fickle popularity changed allegiance from a Republican red to a Democratic blue. Almost overnight, individual candidates emerging from among the leaderless Democrat Party have wrested control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. It was a triumph of right over might, or as its newest star — Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan — put it, the victory of “the many over money”.
Investment in the 2026 midterms has been unprecedented. The final amount is expected to exceed $12 billion, which will be around 30 per cent more than that spent in 2022, and vastly more than the meagre $2bn spent in 2002. Inflation has little to do with it. This year, the top 40 donors contributed $2.5bn, led by the trillionaire Elon Musk. He squandered about $500 million supporting Republican candidates.
There is no Theodore H. White alive to chronicle this electoral extravagance. His book — The Making of the President 1960 — provided a narrative of the rise of the charismatic John F. Kennedy. Unlike Abdul El-Sayed, Kennedy did not have to fight big money. Kennedy’s father was already a millionaire. But, like El-Sayed (a Muslim), Kennedy (a Roman Catholic) had to overcome bitter religious prejudice.
The midterm results were a triumph of right over might.
In September 1960, Kennedy delivered a well-aimed rejoinder to critics who ‘obs­cu­red’ the campaign by questioning his loyalty. He asserted that “the separation of church and state” was absolute. He went further: “I believe in an America that is officially neither Catholic, Protestant, nor Jewish.” He contended that allegiance in America was to the constitution, adding that “no man should be denied public office merely because his religion differs from the president’s”.
The real issues, Kennedy argued, were not his religious faith but hungry children, old people unable to pay medical bills, struggling farmers, insufficient schools, slums, etc. Almost 70 years later, Abdul El-Sayed based his platform on the same issues — schools, healthcare, the cost of groceries, and fuel prices.
El-Sayed owes more, though, to his prototype Barack Hussein Obama. He too was criticised for being a “little bit young, a little bit brown, a little bit Muslim”. Barack Obama was 47 years old when elected president; El-Sayed has just begun his 43rd year. He will be 45 in 2028, when he will foreseeably make his first bid for the presidency. By then, he will have enough credentials.
He will have prompted Trump to end the Israel-incited Iran war and caused a rethink of America’s relationship with Israel. His views on Israel are even-handed: “I believe in equal rights, to peace, dignity, and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike.” He draws a line between Israel and Zionism and he deplores the use of US tax dollars to fund genocide in Gaza, or anywhere else.
Like Obama, El-Sayed is master of the media. He began early. His valedictorian address in 2007 at Michigan University impressed president Bill Clinton enough to earn this compliment: “I wish every person in the world who […] cannot reach across the religious divides, could have heard you speak today.” Clinton advised Abdul El-Sayed to go into politics, despite the burden of his name.
Today, media is not only king; it is the sceptre of presidents. Theodore White analysed that “once Gutenberg put the Bible in print, neither church nor prince could maintain authority [.] Television reached a world that even if it could not read, it could look”. But he warned that, while a president “might control camera at­­t­ention, he could not control events”. Many will remember the slogan that pursued Lyndon B. Johnson over that other undeclared war, in Vietnam: “Hey, hey, LBJ! How many kids did you kill today?”
How will Abdul El-Sayed position himself vis-à-vis Pakistan, as a senator-elect and a president-in-waiting?
Obama visited Pakistan as a student for three weeks in 1981. He learned how to cook local dishes like qeema and dal. He carried away from Pakistan nothing more than recipes and a “changed perspective on economic disparity”.
Abdul El-Sayed has not yet visited Pakistan. Frequently addressing Pakistanis in America, he has called out strongly “for human rights and democratic governance”, drawing a parallel with Egypt (the home of his parents). He cited “its history of military dictatorship” and argued that “neither government should be shielded from criticism, or receive US aid, simply because they are US allies”.
Will Trump and his coterie learn from the results of the US midterm elections? Will they soften in the face of reality, or become increasingly defiant in defeat?
The writer is an author.

title: Homes and hope
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE completion of more than one million homes for families displaced by the 2022 floods is a moment worth celebrating. Behind the figure are stories of loss, perseverance, and fresh beginnings. For those who watched floodwaters sweep away the very lives they had built, a roof means far more than shelter. It means children can sleep, parents can look to the future, and families can move towards a sense of normality. The Sindh Peoples Housing for Flood Affectees programme has now completed 1,007,111 houses across the province, an achievement given the destruction left by the disaster. It is especially encouraging that families have been supported to build homes themselves rather than being treated as recipients of assistance. This gives them a say in shaping the places where they will live. The decision to register homes in women’s names is another welcome move. For many rural women, ownership can bring security and a stronger voice in family affairs.
The milestone also shows what cooperation between provincial authorities, development partners and local communities can accomplish. The challenge was considerable from the outset: Sindh set out to reconstruct 2.1m homes across 23 districts after floods that upended millions of lives. That more than a million have been completed deserves recognition, as does the effort to monitor construction and make houses better able to withstand climate shocks. Yet the occasion should also renew determination to finish the job. Hundreds of thousands of families are still waiting for the same comfort and security. A home, moreover, needs clean water, sanitation, drainage, and access to services if its occupants are to live well. The planned investments in village infrastructure are just as important as the walls and roofs themselves. For now, there is reason for pride. In villages once defined by devastation, families are opening doors to homes they can call their own.

title: History and leadership
author: none@none.com (Shahab Usto)
content:
HISTORY is never linear or monolithic. It may progress in leaps and bounds, or falter and regress. It may appear calm and seamless, but be restive and roiling beneath the surface. No wonder, a small trigger can lead to a cataclysm.
Historians have long debated whether historical dialectics shape human destiny, or human agency lights up the darkest epochs of history. There’s no definite answer as yet. But there is a broad consensus among them on two requisites of a historical ‘development’ — ripe ‘objective’ conditions, and an intelligent leadership that can transform a conducive environment into, at the very least, meaningful change.
Interestingly, the modern era manifests both trends. We see countries and societies long affected by broken governance, endemic corruption, political instability, economic meltdown, civil strife, and regional and global conflagrations. Significant parts of the Middle East, North Africa, and South and West Asia are a dismal reflection of failed or failing states ruled by autocrats or absolutist dynasties — largely without popular mandate and without accountability.
    
Yet there are countries once dismissed as ‘basket-cases’ that have turned themselves around — such as Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam, Turkiye, South Korea, and China. Over the years, they have taken tremendous strides in terms of political stability, socioeconomic progress, scientific and technological advancement, and human-resource development. They have carved out a large share for themselves in international supply chains and productivity.
Much of the credit for their phenomenal achievements goes to their visionary, upright, and courageous political and institutional leadership. True, some of them did not begin as ideal democracies. Yet they built robust, efficient institutions, along with enabling infrastructure, to ensure continuity, stability, peace, and development, and to facilitate a gradual transition to democracy.
In contrast, our state has been stuck in a time warp for decades. Every generation has suffered gross ‘elite capture’ characterised by authoritarianism, disenfranchisement, misgovernance, instability, inequality, impoverishment, and never-ending conflicts. In dialectical terms, although the objective conditions for radical sociopolitical change have long been ripe, the desired agency of change — the political and institutional leadership — has remained elusive.
No wonder the state continues to exist and function in colonial and neocolonial moulds. Authoritarian governance, a compromised and complex legal order, an extractive and iniquitous social structure, the dominance of the security and administrative apparatuses, and a pro-elite neoliberal policy framework remain among its key features.
Our state has been stuck in a time warp for decades.
But has this state worked? Never. The founding ideal of a democratic republic itself has been upended. Instead, a security and administrative juggernaut has been forged on the pretext of guarding national security and ‘ideology’. In fact, the state has been virtually detached from its constitutional and democratic controls. It seeks to draw its power, legitimacy, and even sustenance not from the people’s mandate, but from its coercive powers and capacity to control. Hence, it does not need to worry about citizens’ rights or welfare.
However, this mindset has drawn an ever-widening wedge between the state — controlled and exploited by a small club of security, bureaucratic, political, landed, industrial, and financial elites — and the people, more than half of whom are classified as ‘poor’ or ‘very poor’. Yet, instead of correcting this perilous course, already scarce resources are being further drained for security obligations — arguably, not so much at home as abroad.
    
This raises a disturbing question: for how long can this behemoth, guided by colonial notions of governance and built around failed politico-legal machinery, sustain itself on the proverbial feet of clay — an ever-brittle economy compounded by worsening security and governance failure? This question has arisen in every post-colonial state where elites have captured power, stolen resources, disenfranchised people, and eventually pushed society into chaos and conflict. But in many instances, upright, visionary, and courageous leadership provided the answers — convincingly — by steering the country out of the woods.
Do we have such leadership that can also provide convincing answers — by transforming public angst and alienation towards dysfunctional state structures into a force for building state and political institutions that are democratic, equitable, accountable, and, especially, peace-loving?
Ironically, much of the mainstream political leadership — the PPP, PML-N, PTI, and others — has long forsaken its distinct agenda, and even its identity. Rhetoric aside, they have offered little in the way of ‘answers’ to the many problems afflicting the state and governance. Instead, over the decades, they have tended to outrun one another in their efforts to be more ‘compatible’ with the demands of an extractive state toeing the colonial model.
The PPP-PML-N duo’s joining hands with non-political elements to weaken the judiciary, election commission, and media, and the PTI’s eagerness to mend fences with the powers that be instead of the release of its leader are some recent instances of crass political opportunism and historical compromises on the part of our ‘popular’ leaders.
So, the causes of our recurrent sociopolitical tragedies and the decline of democracy should not be traced to history’s apathy in the face of ominous lengthening shadows. It is the frayed moral fabric of much of our leadership — political and institutional — that gives preference to personal, political, and institutional interests over democracy and the good of the people — the real masters. Under these hopeless circumstances, a new class of self-led movers of history — a sort of Gen-Z — is needed to change our collective destiny.
The writer is a lawyer.
