title: Hidden cause of economic imbalances
author: none@none.com (Shahid Kardar)
content:
GROWING inequality is a serious economic and social issue. Internally, we tend to treat poverty and inequality as separate problems. They are closely connected but not identical. Poverty is about deprivation; inequality is about how income, wealth, opportunities, and economic power are dis­­tributed. An economy can grow and even red­u­­ce poverty temporarily while allowing wealth and privilege to become concentrated. Household data underlines the problem. The consumption-based Gini coefficient increased from 28.4 in 2018 –19 to 32.7 in 2024 –25. This figure does not capture the full extent of inequality in income and wealth, be­­cause household surveys tend to underrepresent the assets and incomes of the richest households.
The distribution of income and wealth influences what people consume, what businesses produce, where investment flows, and how much a country imports. In Pakistan, a relatively small segment commands a disproportionately large share of purchasing power and assets, while much of the population struggles to meet basic needs.
A relatively small segment commands a disproportionately large share of purchasing power and assets.
The benefits of economic growth have been distributed unevenly. Expanding sectors such as banking, telecommunications, IT, energy, oil and gas require capital, technology, and specialised skills, favouring those who already possess financial resources or access to quality education. The state’s failure to provide decent education and healthcare has denied much of the population a fair opportunity to participate in these activities. Hence, economic disadvantages are passed from one generation to the next. Equally damaging is the continued protection of selected businesses from competition through high import duties, subsidies, tax exemptions, and special regulatory concessions. Powerful business groups have resisted competition, sometimes forming cartels to influence prices and markets. Profits earned through state protection rather than efficiency reward influence instead of innovation, raise costs for consumers, and weaken competitiveness.
The tax system has reinforced these inequalities by treating similar incomes from different sources unequally. Salaried individuals face substantial income taxes, while earnings from property, capital gains, and certain commercial activities have historically enjoyed relatively favourable treatment. The state itself has been a major contributor to wealth concentration. Valuable public land and plots have been given to officials and influential individuals, while discretionary powers over building permissions, zoning regulations, and public contracts have created opportunities for private enrichment. Rising property prices, reinforced by speculative investment and the use of real estate to park undeclared wealth, have further increased the fortunes of existing asset owners. Corruption, smuggling, tax evasion, and manipulation of import and export prices have provided additional avenues for accumulating wealth, often beyond the reach of effective taxation and accountability.
Together, these factors constitute a system in which public authority is used to transfer economic opportunities and resources to privileged groups. The consequences extend beyond unfair income distribution; they also distort how the economy allocates and uses its scarce resources.
When fortunes can be made through political connections, regulatory concessions, and protection from competition, capital and entrepreneurial talent are diverted towards securing favours rather than productive investment. It becomes more profitable to lobby for higher import duties or special exemptions than to invest in technology, improve quality, or develop export markets. The concentration of purchasing power also shapes the structure of domestic demand and, therefore, what businesses choose to produce. Businesses often respond to this purchasing power by directing investment towards activities serving a narrow market. Meanwhile, the limited purchasing power of the majority constrains demand for mass-consumption goods, discouraging investment in industries that could serve a broader domestic market, create jobs, and compete globally.
This distorted pattern of consumption and production also contributes to our recurring external imbalances. The concentration of disposable income generates demand for imported vehicles, electronics, luxury goods, foreign travel, and education abroad, adding to the foreign exchange needed for machinery, fuel, technology, and industrial inputs. Not all imports are undesirable. Many are essential for productivity and exports. However, our consumption and production structures generate substantial demand for foreign exchange without a corresponding capacity to earn it through competitive exports. Remittances from overseas Pakistanis have helped bridge this gap. But however valuable these inflows, they cannot substitute indefinitely for an economy capable of financing its import requirements through its own export earnings.
Inequality is certainly not the sole cause of external deficits. Exchange rate policies, tariffs, energy costs, inflation, low productivity, and weak export competitiveness also matter. Still, the concentration of purchasing power helps explain why import demand remains substantial even when we face severe foreign exchange constraints. There is another damaging effect. When influential groups secure tax exemptions, subsidies, and protected markets, government revenues suffer. The burden of financing an oversized, extractive state, with its extensive controls and perks and privileges, consequently falls disproportionately on salaried workers, compliant businesses, and ordinary consumers unable to escape taxation.
Public expenditure compounds the problem. Chronic underinvestment in quality education and healthcare has denied millions of children a fair start. Affluent households can purchase good private education and medical care, while poorer families depend on poor and overstretched public services. Their children’s prospects depend on family circumstances. The failure to provide equal opportunities thereby perpetuates inequality across generations.
Addressing these disparities does not mean pe­­nalising wealth creation. It means distinguishing wealth earned through enterprise, innovation, and productivity from fortunes accumulated through political connections, monopolies, and state-gra­nted privileges. This requires a fairer tax system. Protection must give way to competition, while discretionary allocations of public land, contracts, and regulatory concessions need to be replaced by transparent, rule-based processes. Foreign aid, remittances, and favourable global developments have provided only temporary relief, enabling successive governments to shelve tough reforms, thereby sustaining an economic structure that rewards privilege over productivity.
Unless this system of privileges and unequal opportunities is dismantled, Pakistan will remain trapped in recurring internal and external imbalances, regardless of how many stabilisation programmes it negotiates with the IMF and others.
The writer is a former governor of the State Bank.

title: CT battle
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
IN order to stem the tide of terrorism, it is necessary to ensure that no spaces are left for violent elements to operate in the country. Terrorists often try to blend in with the civilian population. Intelligence-based operations are meant to counter this practice. The military has recently said that two mosques being misused by TTP terrorists in North Waziristan have been cleared. As per ISPR, the terrorists had desecrated the places of worship to store explosives, while also operating torture cells inside the mosques. In the twisted worldview of the TTP and those of their ilk, misusing mosques — as well as attacking the faithful inside places of worship — is acceptable, hence these developments do not come as a surprise. What is important is for operations against violent anti-state elements to continue so that these groups are rooted out for good.
It does seem that the state’s efforts are bearing fruit. According to figures released recently by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, terrorist attacks in October fell by 37pc as compared to September. Improvements were particularly seen in Balochistan and KP — the provinces hardest hit by various strands of terrorism. Yet in KP’s merged districts, where the problem of terrorism is most acute, the gains were modest: October saw 30 attacks compared to 34 in September. Action against terrorist groups must continue until all areas are declared clear of militancy. While the Taliban are reluctant to cooperate against terrorists who launch attacks on Pakistan from Afghan soil, the state here must do all possible to ensure violent elements have no safe spaces within our borders. The gains made over the last month should be capitalised on, with the affected areas permanently cleared of terrorists. These counterterrorism operations must come with minimal displacement of the local people. For over two decades, tribal communities and those living in disturbed areas have faced repeated terrorist violence and displacement due to CT operations. This time the state should ensure that after the terrorism-hit areas are cleared, the government builds on the gains so that local people can live in peace. More IBOs and securing the border against terrorist infiltrators can help bring long-term peace.

Despite gains, challenges persist, particularly in KP's merged districts, requiring sustained operations, border security against infiltrators, and government initiatives for peace and rehabilitation of displaced communities.

title: American dilemma
author: none@none.com (Mahir Ali)
content:
“IRAN militarily is effectively over,” the US president declared on Monday following talks with the Qatari prime minister. “We’re just keeping it the status quo … at the behest” of Iran’s neighbours. The Gulf states include some of Donald Trump’s biggest benefactors, and they have borne the brunt of Iranian military retaliation. Trump has also acknowledged that the domestic unpopularity of the US-Israeli war on Iran contributed to the comprehensive thrashing his Republican Party received in last week’s midterm elections, yet insisted he had no regrets because the goal of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon remained paramount. That’s an absurd premise in a variety of ways; besides, Iran is unlikely to consider the conflict over as long as it is militarily menaced by a superpower or its regional proxies.
What’s notable, though, is that unlike most US aggressions against faraway nations, the majority opinion opposed the assault on Iran from the outset. The co-belligerent’s bloodlust presumably put the kibosh on jingoistic impulses. In a CBS interview on Sunday, Trump admitted that one reason for the midterm drubbing was that “there’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel”. There’s nothing ‘incredible’ about popular distaste for a genocidal power, especially when your tax dollars are enabling its egregious excesses.
It’s true that anti-Israel sentiment paid dividends for candidates across large parts of the US, but the infamous American Israel Public Affairs Committee and other pro-Zionist PACS also scored many successes even as their biggest bets didn’t pay off. AIPAC’s chief bête noire was Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, who in his victory speech thanked the committee, which contributed nearly $40 million to his opponents, for “giving me the opportunity to beat you twice” — in the primary and on election day.
What will the Democrats do with their mandate?
On election eve, Trump announced that nearly $4 billion in annual aid would no longer flow to Israel. That’s unlikely to have affected anyone’s voting intentions, given that presidential pronouncements are notoriously unreliable. But even if there is a halt, far larger avenues of military assistance will remain open, including clauses in the $1.5 trillion 2027 defence budget that effectively embed the Israel Defence Forces in the Pentagon. It’s hard to imagine any serious objections from the AIPAC-aligned Democratic leadership personified by Chuck Schumer in the Senate and Hakeem Jeffries in the House of Representatives.
A growing number of incoming Democratic senators and representatives are keen to dispense with the services of this discredited duo. For the moment though, that’s just wishful thinking. But things could change. The realisation seems to have seeped in that unless the Democrats, with large majorities in both Houses of Congress, begin to deliver on campaign promises, there could be a backlash in 2028. The key issues are mostly domestic, from blatant corruption and the cost of living (exacerbated by the Iran conflict) to healthcare costs, unregulated AI, resource-hungry data centres, and the impunity of tech plutocrats. Elon Musk poured nearly $500m into the midterms, all in vain; he focused on Texas, which turned a bright blue. But the question is whether he can be held to account for his role as head of the now disbanded department of government efficiency, among other misdeeds.
The anti-Trump Republican Congress­man Thomas Massie has already introdu­ced articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth, hoping that Trump will fire him be­­fore the Democrats assume congressio­nal power in January. Massie’s efforts won’t pay off, but will the Democrats do any better? Will they hold Stephen Miller to account for his dedication to deporting ‘illegal aliens’ by brutal means?
Several of the Democrats freshly elected to national office — and many more at the state level — will strive to do their best by their constituents. All too many others, however, have yet to be disabused of the notion that gravitating to the centre is the safest option, even if no measurable progress is achieved. The New York Times editorialised at length on Monday about the wisdom of combining economic ‘populism’ with social conservatism. This is a blueprint for a bridge to nowhere. The Democrats ought to have realised this long ago, but perhaps it’s not too late.
Miller took over as Trump’s chief of staff, indicating a doubling down on his worst impulses, just as the president rescinded his acceptance of last week’s results. It’s a pity that Trump’s invitation to Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White to serve as his press secretary so that the “violent Fighter and Warrior” and his employees could “defend us against the Lunatic Left” turned out to be a joke. Fleetingly, I was reminded of how the Roman emperor Commodus ultimately encountered a wrestler.

title: Values in education
author: none@none.com (Neda Mulji)
content:
SCHOOLS are entrusted with the responsibility of helping students develop their skills to meet the challenges ahead. Skills broadly refer to critical thinking, creativity, communication, and the like. Skills for the future are mostly geared towards developing higher-order thinking so students can become independent and lifelong learners, with curiosity to explore, ability to innovate, and willingness to bring about positive change. Within these parameters is a human side to education — where students’ propensity to respond to what they are taught is closely linked to their affinity with the environment.
Studies show that students benefit from learning when they feel valued by their teachers and peers. Their willingness to contribute in class stems from positive interactions. Globally, as schools work on student and teacher well-being, this phenomenon has become embedded in the school culture. Schools operate as communities, an extension of family, where academic goals are intertwined with shared commitment to goals and values, where there is acceptance of different perspectives. The cue that children get in such an environment is: ‘I matter’. Children with a deep sense of belonging at school know that they will be protected against discrimination and disorder. They know they can speak up in class without being scoffed at, and they are encouraged to demonstrate a sense of purpose and agency. What is the role of teachers in fostering such an environment?
Teachers have long been role models for students. Their words and actions have ripple effects that percolate far down the corridors — from classrooms to common rooms, from the staff rooms to the playground and beyond. Students imbibe communication skills, confidence, rules of engagement, and personal values from their teachers. They watch and learn throughout their school lives. Teachers become carriers of school culture and values. This also means microaggressions can become normalised very quickly. If, for example, a teacher brushes off a student’s comments or reacts angrily to them, the response becomes acceptable to the students, who will demonstrate similar behaviour amongst themselves.
Students benefit from learning when they feel valued.
The human side of education implies looking closely at what the students are learning. What behavioural standards have they come to accept as their own? What expectations do their teachers have of them? Students pick up signals from their environment very early on. Holistic education is not confined to a robust curriculum. It includes values inculcated in classrooms, the mindset and behaviour that define the culture of an educational institution. Schools that have built and sustained a positive culture where students feel valued have done so over time with structured strategies.
Unacceptable social behaviour or incidental infractions are not left unaddressed, nor are there harsh consequences. In fact, research shows that harsh consequences in which students are berated, ostracised, or subjected to humiliation will harden them to the point where they progressively defy authority. The big challenge for students in such environments is not to avoid breaking rules or defying expectations but to perfect the strategies to avoid being caught. The more time a student spends avoiding consequences, the more it affects their overall motivation and ability to focus on academic goals. School life becomes more about avoiding getting into trouble than about doing better in their studies.
School culture and its embedded values are important for this very reason — so students can spend time on actually working on meeting curriculum standa­rds and involving themselves in heal­thy co-curricular and community activities. Students need to spend time em­­bodying the role of responsible citizenship. Many of these values are developed in their foundational years and beyond, mainly through early intervention.
Early intervention can take the form of social-emotional learning that is embedded in the curriculum framework throughout the school years. Students are taught emotional regulation in their interactions, and self-expression and agency in social engagement. Individual strengths are celebrated, personal stories shared, and opportunities created for students’ voices to be heard in small groups and larger forums. When teachers celebrate positive behaviour in public and with parents, students begin to recognise and follow expectations. Some schools provide practical techniques for behaviour reinforcement at home. Many schools organise learning workshops with the senior students so the mantle is carried forward — ‘this is how we do things around here’ is the legacy students imbibe from their seniors and their teachers.
The writer is a teacher educator, author and Fellow of the Higher Education Academy, UK.

title: Opposition moves
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE opposition alliance TTAP has hinted at another anti-government drive. Its recent talks with the JUI-F on parliamentary coordination indicate that the party’s chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman is poised to lead the campaign.
All this raises obvious questions: is the opposition seriously planning an anti-government drive? Is it actually convinced that such a movement at this time can remove the government? Will the pragmatic JUI-F chief join such an effort? At least for now, the answer may disappoint the opposition’s supporters.
The PTI is locked in a protracted battle with the government, while much of its top leadership remains behind bars. It has twice attempted to mobilise public support for a mass movement and rally people around its political objectives since the controversial February 2024 elections, but both attempts failed. It is obvious that people, particularly in Punjab and Sindh, are not ready to join any such movement at this time. Even in KP, where the PTI had been in power since 2013, the party has failed to mobilise the public.
The Jamaat-i-Islami’s drive against high petrol prices similarly failed to bring people out onto the streets.
    
Though the JUI-F has staunch supporters on the streets who are ready to answer their party’s call, its leader has never been one to take needless risks. His azadi march against the PTI government brought thousands of supporters to Islamabad, but failed to dislodge the Imran Khan administration. The sit-in was eventually called off without achieving its objective.
The federal government has imposed emergency measures and governor’s rule in KP, claiming they were necessary for security and administrative reasons. The opposition sees these moves as an assault on provincial autonomy.
Maulana Fazlur Rahman is actively opposing the move. The government’s response to his criticism has fuelled fears that the JUI-F could face the same crackdown as the PTI. Those concerns are not difficult to understand.
    
The recent actions of the Balochistan government against JUI-F Senator Kamran Murtaza on a questionable citizenship claim reinforce these fears. Yet expectations of the maulana leading another street confrontation with the government anytime soon are likely to remain wishful thinking.
Nevertheless, this consensus of politicians of different persuasions reflects a growing frustration with the government’s high-handed actions.
The lawyers’ emergence in this arena is particularly significant. The All Pakistan Lawyers Action Committee in Quetta has vowed to support Senator Murtaza and resist any attempt to undermine constitutional supremacy. There are also reports of raids on lawyers’ homes.
Although the prospects of a new anti-government movement remain remote, public discontent should not be ignored. Small, isolated protests and expressions of dissent can gradually gather momentum and develop into a much larger movement.

title: What money bought
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
SLEAZE, bribery, and secret alliances allegedly marked Trump’s Middle East policy in his first term, and set him on the road to an illegal and unwinnable war against Iran in his second. The central characters in that sordid set of machinations were his own son-in-law and senior adviser Jared Kushner, a few Gulf rulers, and Israel’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu — all working towards a plan to redraw the political map of West Asia. Iran was the adversary to be contained, and it was on this that they converged: a plan to “blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal”.
Billions of dollars were allegedly paid to Kushner in what may be the biggest scandal in recent history — one that best defines the link between money and Trump’s conduct of his Middle East policy, and which has pushed the entire region into an intractable conflict with global consequences.
A recently published book, Princes and Thieves by investigative journalist Matthew Cole, provides startling details on how billions of dollars were allegedly transferred into accounts — managed by Kushner — by Gulf sheikhdoms, to implement a plan to break Obama’s nuclear deal with Iran and change the “political map of the Middle East”. The author supports his view of the transactions with details drawn from accounts hacked by a Western intelligence agency, though Kushner has called the allegations fabricated.
According to the author, the transfers began in 2017 and were well underway by the spring of 2018, during Trump’s first term — when Kushner served as the president’s special envoy on the Middle East. While he had very close relations with Israel, he also cultivated strong business and diplomatic connections with willing Gulf sheikhdoms to allegedly pay for influence with the Trump administration.
>A recent book details how money and corruption were leveraged to redesign the Middle East.
According to the author, “Kushner, UAE ruler Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ), and Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) of Saudi Arabia, converged at an auspicious moment. MBS wanted to be crown prince. MBZ wanted to blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, and Kushner wanted both to help him force the Palestinians into a deal that Israel would accept”. The convergence against Obama’s nuclear deal with Iran — formally the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) — brought Saudi Arabia and the UAE together on the issue.
Agreed on July 14, 2015, between Iran and the P5+1, and endorsed by Security Council Resolution 2231, the deal came into effect in January 2016. Under it, Iran capped its enrichment at 3.67 per cent, cut its centrifuge numbers and opened its nuclear facilities to IAEA inspection. In return, nuclear-related sanctions on Iran were lifted on oil exports, banking, and SWIFT access, with frozen assets to be released in stages.
But Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE had strong reservations. Each opposed the JCPOA for different reasons and with different intensity; the common ground was that the agreement was too narrow and too temporary, its restrictions written to expire under sunset clauses. Israel openly campaigned against it, and the two Gulf states lobbied against it too.
For deal sceptics, Trump’s election in 2016 was good news. In May 2018, the president withdrew from the JCPOA and reimposed sanctions in phases under a “maximum pressure” campaign. The move brought the Gulf nations closer to the Trump administration. The billions alleged to have flowed into Kushner’s accounts appeared to have delivered. The book maintains that early in Trump’s first term, “MBZ and MBS offered to pay for a slush fund dedicated to helping the new administration with foreign policy goals”. Both Arab rulers saw this as part of an effort to help Trump win a second presidency.
In the same period, Kushner conceived the so-called Abraham Accords aimed at normalisation between Israel and the Arab states. He owned the file. No State Department desk, no regional bureau, no ambassador in the chain: a son-in-law with a security clearance and a direct line to the president negotiated directly with the Gulf rulers, according to the book. One goal was to sideline the question of a separate Palestinian state. The UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan signed.
The book also reveals that during that period Kushner helped negotiate a secret warming of diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE — the arrangement that later became public as the Abraham Accords. Cole writes that “Kushner helped negotiate an agreement by Israel to help defend the UAE against a major Iranian military attack. The UAE needed to cover the cost of that emergency defence, and its government secretly made another transfer to Israel’s Central Bank. This was something like a rainy-day defence fund. Combined, the three accounts represented a secret foreign policy negotiated by Kushner with the leaders of Israel, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia.
“Although Kushner’s position as senior adviser to the president was unpaid, he was an official government employee. Not only did his position require financial disclosure for ethics regulations, but each year he worked in the White House he had to file both a public and a confidential financial form, the Executive Branch Personnel Public Financial Disclosure Report, known as a 278e disclosure. Because he had access to classified government secrets, Kushner was required to disclose any bank account to which he had signatory — or beneficiary — access.” But apparently, the president’s son-in-law did not comply.
The writer quotes a source that Kushner “promised MBZ he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalisation with Israel so that business could take off”. For the Gulf Arab governments, money was not a problem. “The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent,” the source told the author.
The book exposes the sordid linkage between power and corruption that marked Trump’s presidency. It also lays bare the unholy alliance between Israel and the Gulf governments, formed to change the political map of the Middle East. In the end, this design has left the region more destabilised than before.
The writer is an author and journalist.

title: Economic ills
author: none@none.com (Dr Niaz Murtaza)
content:
DESPITE an oversold stabilisation, many of our economy’s vital signs continue to falter. The economy resembles a patient out of the ICU but still in hospital.
Since 2024, our per capita GDP growth has been near zero — sadly, South Asia’s slowest recorded pace. Even our recent growth spurts, brief and import-led, have given way to longer busts, draining reserves and sending us back to the IMF’s tough terms that extend low growth.
Once near the region’s top performers in per capita GDP, we now risk falling to the bottom. As incomes stall, poverty rises. Our extreme poverty rate (23 per cent) is near the bottom regionally. It’s about 10 times India’s, against near parity in 2011.
Our GDP’s composition tells a bleak tale too. It’s consumption-heavy (82pc) but investment-light (14pc) — on both counts among the region’s worst. India and China invest over 30pc of GDP, creating jobs and capacity for today and later — much better than our consumption binges. Limiting job, technology, and export growth, industry’s share has been nearly a fifth for over 50 years versus a quarter in India and Sri Lanka and a third in Bangladesh.
    
Low investment causes low growth, but its origins and destinations matter too. We court foreign capital while ignoring local capital. Foreign capital must earn and save more dollars than it repatriates and create jobs and local capacity. But we get it mostly in domestic sectors, which later depletes reserves.
Unlike our peers, we chase a few rich states for capital rather than prioritising diversified private capital. We shun creative ways to boost local savings and capital. So, we remain capital-starved — yet we quickly drain reserves and risk the haughty whims of rich states.
Capital droughts in export sectors cause dollar and job droughts. From a peak of 17pc in 1992, exports now barely reach a tenth of our GDP — South Asia’s second-lowest share, below even Afghanistan’s. Low-quality compounds low quantity. Harvard’s Economic Complexity Index ranks us 89th among 145 states. So our exports face intense competition but return little. Exports rarely cover imports, creating large trade gaps.
Dreary metrics mirror a sinking economy.
Remittances partly plug the gap. But exports keep workers at home and families intact, create jobs, earn dollars, and pay taxes.
Remittances separate families and often don’t create jobs or pay taxes directly. They frequently fuel consumption, while exports are fuelled by investment. Remittances now almost equal our exports, as it is easier to send workers abroad than goods (India earns six times as much from exports as from remittances). Even so, we often run large external deficits that lead to a crisis as booms turn into busts.
Low growth and weak efforts leave our coffers lean. Tax revenues barely reach 11pc of GDP — which is among South Asia’s lowest. Indirect anti-poor taxes provide about half our tax target, down from about two-thirds in 2021-22. New direct taxes further burden the wallets of salaried persons and formal industry, while favoured sectors pay low taxes. Spending prioritises upkeep over uplift. Expenditure hogs over 90 paisas out of every federal budget rupee; development consoles itself with just five.
These twin deficits force us to keep our borrowing bowl out. Our public debt-to-GDP ratio of 73pc is lower than the Japanese and Singaporean levels of over 150pc. But our repayment muscle better depicts our debt overhang.
    
On the share of federal outlays spent on interest alone, we rank among the worst globally. We use debt not only to invest or meet recurrent expenses but also to beef up rese­rves. IMF debt and deposits by rich states, which impose odious economic and political conditions on us, now exceed even our highest-ever reserves. These dre­ary metrics mirror a sinking economy. Low investment and import-led growth widen the twin deficits to swell debt. Interest outlays then leave little money for growth, creating a vicious circle.
A weak economy reflects perverse politics. Poor countries need both a developmental and a welfare state. Ours is a parasitic and apathetic state run by rapacious rulers. This isn’t a tragedy of ineptitude alone: willing rulers can easily hire merit. It’s a deliberate design by kleptocrats who may lose their wealth and power if there is real progress.
Nor is this the tale of a few eras. Our autocracies, too, delivered short-term growth, leading to conflict and undercutting future progress. Ideas abound on how to pursue sound progress, but minds that will champion and implement them well do not. Only democracy and civilian sway will bring such minds to the helm of affairs.
The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 30 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.

title: Terrorism and the writ of the state
author: Dr Syed Akhtar Ali Shah
content:
Persistent terrorism in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa has inflicted a heavy toll on human life while devastating the region's economy and social fabric - a trend showing no signs of abating. Why does this violence persist despite various counterterrorism strategies and the immense sacrifices of police, security personnel and civilians? The writ of the state cannot be assessed merely by cleared territory or militants killed. The real test is whether citizens can work, travel, attend school, and seek justice without fear.

Recent acts of terror amplify the scale of the challenge. At Speen Mela in Hassan Khel, militants assaulted a police post, martyring Constable Muhammad Jalal and injuring three others. In another incident, five policemen were injured in an attack on the Gumbati checkpost in Bannu. Additional SHO Meera Khan was also shot dead near Miranshah. On October 22, CTD DSP Imranuddin Khan, SHO Afzal Awan and two fellow policemen were martyred in a Karak ambush, which also left two militants dead.

Civilian life remains equally fraught with danger. In one incident, armed militants abducted 17 project and sugar mill workers who remain missing. Such lawlessness carries consequences far beyond the immediate victims; industry cannot flourish where kidnapping and coercion make travel unsafe. Meanwhile, in South Waziristan, a mortar shell struck a house in Toi Khulla, killing three civilians and injuring five. The origin of the shell has yet to be established.

Moreover, in Bannu, a roadside motorcycle bomb exploded near a police patrol, injuring two civilians. Similarly, unverified social media reports indicated that three children were wounded in a quadcopter attack in Bannu on October 23, while a civilian was shot and killed by unidentified gunmen in Bajaur that same day. Together, these unabated acts have intensified the pervasive sense of insecurity.

These incidents and sacrifices, deeply interlinked with the past, require more than just ceremonial tributes; they demand a rigorous review of intelligence, equipment, tactics and operational reinforcements. Against the backdrop of intensified attacks, Malik Khan Marjan, Vice Chairman of the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC), has proposed sending a delegation of 15 to 20 authorised tribal elders to Afghanistan to negotiate with the TTP, Hafiz Gul Bahadur's group, and other factions. The urgency behind his appeal is understandable. Communities devastated by decades of violence are desperate to adopt any means necessary to normalise the situation.

However, this proposal is highly questionable and contradicts national counterterrorism policy. Moreover, relying on tribal chiefs to resist organised militant networks - backed by heavy weaponry, funding, territorial networks and ideological command structures - is an exercise in self-deception. The historical record is highly alarming. Data from the South Asia Terrorism Portal reveals that at least 194 tribal elders were killed in 143 separate incidents between 2005 and March 2024. This targeted campaign has severely weakened local resilience and fractured the region's social fabric. Crucially, these figures reflect inherently incomplete media reporting and represent an absolute minimum rather than an exhaustive total.

A significant number of tribal elders who opposed militancy and sided with the government were systematically targeted and killed. For instance, former Senator Malik Faridullah Khan Wazir and two other elders were assassinated in Jandola in 2005. Decades of targeted assassinations, extortion and intimidation have severely eroded traditional authority, silenced local resistance and rendered collective action extremely dangerous. Given this historical pattern, expecting unprotected community representatives to confront highly organised militant groups is an unsound proposition that is unlikely to yield the desired results.

Temporary ceasefires and peace agreements in the past have failed to deliver lasting peace. A government-sponsored tribal jirga helped secure a TTP ceasefire announcement in 2022, but capitulating to their core demands - including the reversal of the former FATA merger - amounted to surrendering the writ of the state, causing the truce to eventually collapse. Any renewed engagement must strictly specify who authorises negotiators, guarantees safety, verifies compliance and ensures that militants cannot exploit pauses to regroup. Crucially, victims, women and affected local communities must not be excluded from decisions that directly shape their security.

Although Malik Marjan's call for dialogue may seem like a personal opinion, given the fact that he is the Vice Chairman of the newly formed ARDC and thus a public face of the government administration, his remarks cannot be easily brushed aside. However, the state policy must remain completely unambiguous and must never abdicate its constitutional responsibilities.

The state's strategy must clearly distinguish between organised militant groups, with their distinct operational patterns, and ordinary criminal gangs. Effective counterterrorism requires integrated intelligence, highly capable Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) units, sound investigations and credible prosecutions. Furthermore, it demands the sustained protection of roads, schools and businesses, alongside - above all - filling the critical gaps in local governance.

Under the 25th Constitutional Amendment, a considerable journey has been undertaken toward administrative, political and judicial integration; however, full financial integration has yet to materialise. Consolidating these reforms requires the provision of finances as mandated by the NFC mechanism under the Constitution of Pakistan.

To properly gauge the security environment, the state must regularly publish verifiable monthly figures on attacks, casualties, kidnappings, extortion cases, investigations and convictions, alongside measurable outcomes for civilian safety. Transparency, accountability and the public welfare - expressed in measurable terms - are indispensable for good governance. While traditional leadership can contribute to localised peace, imagining that vulnerable elders can neutralise sophisticated militant networks misinterprets history and abdicates the core responsibilities of the state. Ultimately, this threat must be tackled directly by the organised force of the state.

title: Extreme heat
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
CLIMATE change is already taking its toll on Pakistan’s farm sector. Crop yields are falling, livestock productivity is declining, fertile land is becoming uncultivable, and food insecurity is rising. Alongside, rural incomes are shrinking, and both cash and food poverty are increasing. It is against this backdrop that a new UN assessment — Extreme Heat and Agriculture — by the Food and Agriculture Organisation and the World Meteorological Organisation has sought to underscore the rapid erosion of farm productivity, especially in rain-fed regions, and its impact on rural households owing to rising temperatures across the country. The findings are particularly worrying for Punjab, where frequent and severe heatwaves are disrupting rural livelihoods. Fruit productivity in the province’s high-rainfall areas has halved. Livestock is suffering, with heat stress reducing milk production and increasing the incidence of diseases among small ruminants. The consequences are not confined to farms. Lower output means reduced incomes for farming households, with extreme temperatures accelerating the spoilage of vegetables, dairy products, and other perishables. Families earn and eat less. Gender inequality deepens the problem. Rural women, who undertake considerable agricultural and household work, face prolonged exposure to extreme temperatures. Pregnant and lactating women are particularly vulnerable, with a sharp increase in the risk of premature births during severe heatwaves.
However, climate adaptation is yet to find a place in our agricultural policies. The effects of rising temperatures on the sector that sustains two-thirds of the population cannot be mitigated with input subsidies, crop support prices, or procurement targets. Farmers need heat-resistant crop varieties, better water management technology, and access to modern farming machinery. Investment in cold storage, efficient supply chains and public and livestock health services is equally important. Agricultural research requires greater private investment and better human resources. Without tweaking policies to respond to the climate challenge, repeated heatwaves will erode productivity, making farming less viable for smallholders. The problem crosses the border. Both sides of Punjab face the same climate challenges, requiring Pakistan and India to cooperate on farm resilience. Heat is already cutting into rural incomes and into what families can afford to eat. Farm policies that ignore it will fail the people they are meant to support.

Current agricultural policies (e.g., input subsidies, crop support prices) are inadequate; a paradigm shift towards climate adaptation, including heat-resistant crops, better water management, cold storage, and increased research investment, is essential.

The socio-economic consequences extend beyond farms, exacerbating gender inequality and impacting vulnerable groups, while policy inaction risks making farming unviable for smallholders and necessitates cross-border cooperation.

title: Missing discussion
author: none@none.com (Naseer Memon)
content:
IN contrast to official claims of economic stability, a series of recently released reports provide disturbing evidence of deepening poverty and a human development crisis in Pakistan.
According to the World Bank’s Pakistan Poverty and Equity brief, the national poverty rate spiralled from 22 per cent in 2018-19 to 29pc in 2024-25 — meaning that about 70 million poor people across the country live below the national poverty line. The Gini index, a measure of economic inequality, has increased from 28.4pc to 32.7pc, the highest in 25 years. The World Bank’s regional economic outlook reported that Pakistan is home to about half of the MENAAP region’s population that falls under the extremely poor category. The World Bank attributes Pakistan’s reversal in poverty reduction to economic shocks triggered by the Covid-19 pandemic, the devastating 2022 floods, high inflation, and currency depreciation.
The UNDP’s 2025 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index reported that 38.3pc of Pakistan’s population (95m people) is multidimensionally poor — deprived not just of cash but also of necessities such as healthcare and education. Another 32m people are vulnerable to multidimensional poverty. Pakistan’s poor population of 38.3pc dwarfed India’s 16.4pc and Bangladesh’s 14.9pc.
The alarming scale of deprivation was also reflected in the 2026 Global Hunger Index, which placed Pakistan 106th among 122 countries. Pakistan has the highest hunger score in South Asia. The report attributes food price inflation to declining household purchasing power and constrained access to food. It finds that undernourishment in the country climbed from ‘low’ in 2018 to ‘medium’, while child wasting has risen towards the ‘high’ threshold.
Poverty is rooted in decades of misguided public policy.
All these reports reflect the severity of the crisis. A nationally representative mental health survey (2018-22), published in the British Medical Journal, revealed distressing facts. The survey found that every third Pakistani lives with a diagnosable mental or behavioural disorder; one in five meets the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder. A shocking 6pc reported suicidal thoughts, and more than one in 10 had depression. Such staggering rates of mental disorders have been linked to lower income and poor education, unemployment, age, and disrupted family circumstances.
Human development has remained a chronically ignored priority in Pakistan. The UNDP’s Human Development Report 2025 placed Pakistan 168th out of 193 countries appearing in the ‘low’ human development category. Except for Afghanistan, all regional countries ranked ahead of Pakistan on the Human Development Index.
Poverty is rooted in decades of misguided public policy and bad governance. Human development has been given cosmetic importance — the subject is mostly confined to official speeches and election manifestos. Although Covid-19, the floods, and broader climate change have battered the economy, human development seldom features on the government’s list of priorities. Geopolitical and ongoing border tensions, and more recently the Gulf war shocks, have diverted resources and attention from human development to security priorities. The issue has been further compounded by internal security challenges that have held back exports and stifled foreign investment. Terrorism in two provinces and the poor law and order situation have shattered local investments. This environment has forced many foreign companies to pack up and withdraw capital from our markets.
Agriculture — for long the bedrock of the national economy and a source of food security for millions — has been systematically eroded in recent decades. Sha­rp increases in agri-input prices, a poorly managed water sector, rapid land degradation, and exploitative market forces have wrecked this critical sector. Soaring energy prices, an unreliable grid, and a huge tax burden, including petroleum surcharges, have made energy exorbitant for the farm sector. Crippling increases in petroleum prices have pushed up transport fares, raising the cost of the farm-to-market supply chain. The resulting food inflation has forced millions of families to compromise on their diet.
Sadly, even though poverty and hunger have emerged as an existential challenge for millions of families in Pakistan, a national focus on these issues is absent. These issues rarely find space in the national discourse — especially on electronic media, which remains abuzz with hysterical talk shows on subjects like governor’s rule and new provinces. Distracting the masses from the real issues and failing to include critical report findings will not reduce the citizens’ frustration.
The writer is senior adviser, water governance, at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute.

title: Rice straw can yield clean energy rather than smog
author: Web Desk
content:
Pakistan is the tenth largest rice producer in the world and the fourth largest exporter. According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (2024-2025), Pakistan produced more than 9.8 million tonnes of rice grain, while around 13 million tonnes of rice straw was generated when harvested manually or by machines. However, rice straw is currently underutilised because of its low nutritional value and high percentage of silica, making it unsuitable for animal feed. Rice straw is burnt due to no commercial value and due to constraints in collection of straw from field because of high associated costs or time constraints issues for the next crop sowing. Rice straw is sometimes fired for household heating or for cooking in rural areas.

In recent years, straw burning has become a major environmental issue as it not only pollutes the environment but also degrades the soil ecology, affecting the nutrient availability in soil. Intensive rice straw burning occurs within 2 to 4 weeks (mid of October to mid of November) in Pakistan. The burning of rice straw creates various environmental problems, including high GHGs emissions, aerosol particles, such as coarse dust particles (PM10) and fine particles (PM2.5), and toxic gases, such as carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Smog formation occurs due to high amounts of VOCs and nitrogen oxides, which react in the presence of sunlight to form ground-level ozone, which can affect weather conditions. This can further exacerbates environmental conditions when there is no rain during these conditions, resulting in heavy smog.

The world is moving toward a bio circular economy, which is a closed-loop system that replaces fossil fuel-based products with renewable, bio-based materials, primarily from agricultural, forestry, and marine waste, and then cycles these materials back into the economy to minimise waste and pollution. It is a shift towards a nature-powered economy that aims to regenerate natural systems by using natural capital, thereby reducing dependence on non-renewable resources and supporting sustainable well-being.

Pakistan is burning valuable crop residues, such as rice straw, to convert them into issues such as depletion of soil organic matter, environmental pollution, human health toxic smog and fossil fuel energy import bills. According to a study on rice straw valorisation published in the Environmental Science and Pollution Research journal, raw rice straw can be challenging to convert into biogas using specialised microbes. However, this biogas can be purified by removing impurities to produce biomethane, which shares similar applications with natural gas. Biomethane can then be utilised in existing natural gas infrastructure or converted into Liquefied Natural Gas (Bio-LNG). Demand for Bio-LNG is currently soaring, especially as a maritime fuel.

However, lead researcher Muhamamad Abdul Hanan Siddhu notes that approximately 126 m³ of biomethane can be produced per tonne of rice straw through anaerobic digestion, while the biomethane yield can be significantly increased to 205 m³/tonne (63%) of rice straw by developing special techniques and emerging steam explosion pretreatment technology. A subsequent calculation showed that the use of Siddhu's steam explosion pretreatment technology to convert approximately 80% of Pakistan's burned rice straw could produce 2133 million m³ of biomethane or 1.5 million tonnes of Bio-LNG, accounting for 8532 million units of electricity, which could meet the energy demand of roughly 3.7 million households. Steam explosion pretreatment technology is chemical-free, and after harnessing the biomethane potential from rice straw, the residue can be utilised as fertiliser in agricultural production systems to reduce the dependency on expensive imported synthetic inputs and mitigate environmental problems and associated human health risks.

Therefore, the government should promote and support advanced and emerging environment-friendly technologies, such as steam explosion pretreatment, to valorise rice straw into biomethane production and simultaneously mitigate smog, reduce environmental issues and conserve Pakistan's natural resources and its foreign reserves.

title: Served by the court
author: none@none.com (Arifa Noor)
content:
LAST week, the newly established Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) gave two noteworthy judgements. Both concerned legal issues of a political nature — the kind that perhaps would have taken up considerable time and energy in the Supreme Court of the olden days, along with detailed coverage by the media. But those were different times; at present, the cases progressed quietly and the decisions came without much bang or thunder.
In one case, the court settled an election dispute that has been going on for the past two years. Back in 2024, the JUI-F had disputed the notification of a woman to one of its reserved seats. It claimed that the woman who had been notified simply shared the first name — Sadaf — with the woman mentioned on the party’s list. The woman on the JUI-F list, Sadaf Yasmin, had decided against submitting her papers due to personal reasons; however, a woman called Sadaf Ihsan (with whom the party says it has no connection) submitted her papers and got nominated by the ECP for the seat. The JUI-F claims Ihsan impersonated Sadaf Yasmin despite having a different name and was somehow identified as the latter.
When this was pointed out to the Election Commission of Pakistan, not only did it withdraw the announcement, but also suspended the official who issued the notification. This was reported in Dawn. But the matter didn’t end there. Sadaf Ihsan approached the Peshawar High Court (PHC) and was reinstated. The party then challenged the decision in the Supreme Court, winning reprieve for itself. Ihsan was suspended. But the relief was simply an interim order, and once the FCC was established, the file was transferred to it.
The FCC sent the case back to the ECP, which in January this year reinstated Sadaf Ihsan in the seat. This past week, the JUI-F’s appeal against this decision was dismissed by the FCC. Ihsan is now a JUI-F MNA, while the party continues to insist that she is not a member and was never on the list submitted to the ECP. Ihsan, according to a report on the Fafen website, claims she and her family are associated with the party.
Three cases, three judgements. But they reveal quite a lot of what the court appears to stand for.
It now appears the decision is final and no appellate forums remain. Another interesting aspect of this case is that this seat was given to the JUI-F after the decision that deprived the PTI of reserved seats.
In a second case, the FCC has apparently stopped the PHC from hearing cases regarding the custody or arrest of PTI workers. With the imposition of the emergency in KP and a crackdown against the party in the province, multiple cases concerning the whereabouts or bail of PTI members ended up in the PHC, which then passed an interim order preventing such detentions.
As in many cases, bail had also been granted; the provincial government challenged them in the FCC. According to one report in Dawn, more than 60 cases in which bail had been given were challenged by the KP government in the FCC. After hearing the cases, the FCC stopped the high court from hearing these matters; its argument was that since the army has been called in, in aid of civil power, the court could no longer hear matters under Article 199, which, in layperson’s terms, is equivalent to what we once saw as the suo motu powers of the Supreme Court.
    
According to one lawyer’s comment, which he posted on social media, this order means the high court can no longer entertain any writ petitions, which, according to him, is a power the courts continued to enjoy even under martial law regimes. In other words, the order limits the PHC in matters far wider than simply the arrests of and bail for PTI workers. It means the high court cannot hear any matters related to fundamental rights.
While these two cases date back to just the past week, a third judgement is a little older. It had already been discussed in quite a bit of detail in Dawn and elsewhere. But it is still worth mentioning.
    
In a recent case, the FCC seems to have provided a restricted interpretation of workplace harassment. Ignoring past precedents, which had interpreted workplace harassment more liberally, the court has now ruled that harassment is to be limited to actions of an overtly sexual nature; previously, judgements had interpreted the law to include what is defined as gender-based discrimination.
A piece by Barrister Rida Hosain pointed out that in a previous decision, Justice Ayesha Malik had said that “reducing harassment to conduct that is sexual in nature ‘takes away the essence’ of the harassment law, and ignores that harassment is often less about sexual interest and more about reinforcing existing power dynamics”. Hosain quoted Justice Ayesha Malik as saying that the very “purpose of harassment laws is to address gender-based discrimination at the workplace and not to limit it to sexual forms of harassment”. But the FCC has now seen it differently.
And while the decision drew criticism, it is fortunate that amendments to the law itself have provided a more wide-ranging definition. However, the ruling of the FCC does mean that complainants in incidents or cases that predate the amendment may have to prove harassment according to the FCC’s interpretation. Women lawyers in particular have discussed this issue in detail in articles and commentary that have appeared in Dawn.
Three cases, three judgements. But they reveal quite a lot of what the FCC appears to stand for — to those of us who have little understanding of the legalese but who do keep an eye on the politics of the country — be it fundamental rights, women’s rights, or perhaps those of political parties. One can only wonder if any of the parliamentarians who voted for these courts have paid any attention to these judgements.
The writer is a journalist.
Published in Dawn, November 10th, 2026

title: Restructuring plans
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
NO matter how strongly the PPP, a key coalition partner, wishes to see it buried, the push for new administrative units and provinces seems to be picking up steam once again.
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif brought the issue into the limelight on Sunday, telling an interviewer that the country could have as many as 12 new provinces if the exercise were driven by administrative needs rather than ethnic, linguistic, or political considerations. Yet in Pakistan, redrawn boundaries always carry ethnic and political weight.
Speculation about a possible administrative restructuring has intensified of late, with talk of it soon being accomplished through a 28th amendment to the Constitution. It is also suggested that while the amendment may be fast-tracked, perhaps wrapped up within the year, its actual implementation will be deferred until after the next general election because of the formidable legal and administrative challenges involved in redistributing the state’s resources equitably.
But if the implementation can wait, why not the legislation?
    
The government may be tempted to push ahead while it can still count on a majority in parliament, but a majority alone is not a consensus. A proposal of such immense national import demands nothing less.
The Election Commission’s botched conduct of the 2024 general election has also left serious, lingering doubts about how far the current legislature represents the public will — doubts that might taint any constitutional change of this magnitude that it passes. It would, therefore, be a much wiser move, politically speaking, to take up any debate on administrative restructuring again after the next general election.
In the interim, parliament should pursue electoral reforms with the opposition to ensure that the commission does not repeat its 2024 mistakes, so that the next election earns the public’s trust and yields a legislature whose mandate is beyond doubt.
Until then, the federal and provincial governments should at least make an effort to revive the local government structure and give it a fair chance to prove its efficacy as a means of public service delivery.
    
Most arguments in favour of new administrative units circle back to a few central ideas, chief among which is the failure of provincial governments to ensure that resources allocated to them reach the people. The LG system was designed to be that last-mile tier of governance that would make this possible, but, sadly, successive civilian governments have failed to operationalise it effectively, preferring instead to concentrate administrative, political and financial power in a few provincial centres.
Population growth and internal migration have sharply increased pressures on existing administrative centres in recent decades, but empowered LGs can redistribute that burden without redrawing provincial boundaries.
It is up to the political leadership to choose between these two paths.
Published in Dawn, November 10th, 2026

title: Flight from reality
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
PAKISTAN’S ruling elites devote inordinate time and attention to foreign engagements — at the expense of tackling domestic challenges. The country’s media also tends to focus more on foreign policy and international events than on fundamental problems confronting the country. Switch on any TV channel and most talk shows are endlessly discussing Pakistan’s overseas forays, defence agreements, and other global developments. Some of this is understandable as a war in the neighbourhood and regional and international dynamics do have implications for Pakistan that merit comment. But domestic issues more consequential to the country’s fate and future rarely receive the same attention.
There may be several reasons for this. For ruling elites, foreign engagements are a way to access and collect geopolitical rents to keep the economy afloat, enabling them to avoid undertaking domestic reform. Their notion of ‘success’ rests on foreign alignments that can deliver these rents without having to expend political energy solving structural economic problems at home. Hence, the almost obsessive focus on foreign pursuits and lack of reform at home.
For governments resting on dubious electoral mandates, it is also the means to acquire international legitimacy to compensate for its absence at home. This is more so for authoritarian and hybrid regimes. There is also more cachet in taking overseas trips and having photo-ops with world leaders than trying to get ministries to do their job. That is why ministers often spend more time abroad than in the country, with prime ministers exceeding their predecessors’ record of foreign visits. Fixing the country’s problems is much harder than flying off to, say, Davos. A cynical explanation is that the country’s problems — poverty, hunger, lack of education, and health facilities, malnutrition, growing population numbers — don’t affect the power elite, so if they fester there is no skin off its back. Certainly, it sees no urgency in addressing them.
Pakistan’s future will be determined at home, not abroad.
The excessive attention that much of Pakistan’s broadcast media devotes to foreign policy and external developments is explained by other factors. The obvious one is the electronic media simply covers what the country’s leadership is doing. But it also means it is content to play follow-my-leader and not set its own agenda that takes public issues into account. Discussing foreign trips and events involves far less effort than delving into complex domestic issues. Confrontations between the government and opposition do get plenty of coverage. But when a report on an aspect of Pakistan’s economic and social situation is published, the coverage and discussion are fleeting and shallow, with no analysis or follow-up. There are occasional exceptions but an in-depth analysis or investigative documentary on a consequential socioeconomic issue is hard to come by. Above all, TV channels seem to believe serving up formulaic talk shows is enough for viewers.
Yet issues that warrant the attention of primarily the government, that can do something about them, and media, which can encourage authorities to pay attention, have become even more urgent. Improving the living conditions of people is the government’s most important task. That it has not lived up to this task is apparent from the fact that poverty, for example, has risen significantly in recent years. According to the World Bank, Pakistan’s national poverty rate rose from 22 per cent in 2018-19 to 29pc in 2024-25. The WB also estimates that Pakistan accounts for almost half of the poor in the 23 countries of the MENAAP region (Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan). UNDP estimates 38.3pc of Pakistan’s population face multidimensional poverty, which measures multiple, overlapping deprivations in education, health, and standard of living that go beyond a purely monetary standard of poverty.
So why is the government unable to deal with the increasing number of people living below the poverty line? It is argued that the government is constrained by the macroeconomic situation and an IMF programme that is contractionary, and has to focus on stabilising the economy. But that should not prevent it from addressing poverty. There is much that can be done to reduce poverty that has nothing to do with the spending cycle. After all, the IMF hardly prevents the government from allocating resources judiciously, mobilising revenue, pursuing non-tax filers, and curbing electricity theft. Stabilising the economy has nothing to do with vanity projects undertaken at the expense of helping the poor.
Poverty is also reflected in the alarming state of hunger in the country. Pakistan is among the world’s 10 countries where millions face acute hunger, according to an international humanitarian organisation, Action Against Hunger. Another recent report, No Security Without Food Security, finds Pakistan is worst hit by hunger in South Asia. Deteriorating food insecurity is attributed to economic instability, inflation, and climate shocks. Malnutrition associated with poverty is also responsible for child stunting. Around 40pc of Pakistani children under five are stunted, which condemns them to a life of physical disability, poverty, and lifelong deprivation.
No issue matters more to the country’s future than education. Yet it barely gets priority attention from the government. Pakistan still has the world’s second highest number of out-of-school children, around 25m (aged five to 16) — over half of them girls. This is a national scandal. Literacy remains stagnant, with 37pc of people illiterate. No country can make economic progress with that level of illiteracy. Without investment in people, economic growth will remain elusive. The education deficit is all the more serious given the youth bulge. Over two-thirds of the population are below age 30. The young will determine the country’s destiny. But if they are uneducated and unemployable, they face a hopeless future. This jeopardises the country’s prospects. Also disturbing is the share of youth (15-29 years) who are not in education, employment, and training, known as the NEET rate, which is 37pc overall and 62pc for women, according to a Gallup report.
Human capital and human development, crucial for economic growth, have suffered from government indifference and deteriorated over time. Foreign engagements count for little when there is no improvement in the condition of the majority of people. Nor does the ‘glamour’ of foreign trips obscure the grim reality of the economic and social deprivations people face across the country. Nation-building at home should have priority. Pakistan’s future, after all, will be determined at home, not abroad.
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
Published in Dawn, November 9th, 2026

title: Antalya agenda
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
WHEN COP31 opens in Antalya today, governments will have to show that years of climate negotiations have produced more than ambitious targets and promises of financial help. Geopolitical tensions, an energy crisis, and strained finances in rich countries have dampened hopes of a breakthrough. The absence of an official US delegation after Washington’s withdrawal from the Paris Agreement has worsened matters. Meanwhile, the climate crisis is advancing faster than efforts to contain it. A new UN report warns that even if countries fulfil existing climate pledges, global temperatures could rise by 2.6°C this century. For Pakistan, already exposed to floods, extreme heat, and erratic rainfall, the question is what it can realistically secure from the talks. At COP29, developed countries committed to mobilising $300bn annually for developing nations by 2035. COP30 called for progress towards a broader goal of $1.3tr a year and for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035. But promises of more money mean little if vulnerable states cannot access it.
For Pakistan, the priority should be to secure easier access to climate funds, more grants rather than debt-creating loans, and clear deadlines for financial contributions. It should seek support for practical measures to protect homes from flooding, secure water supplies, and improve early warning systems. By joining forces with other vulnerable countries, Pakistan could strengthen calls for better glacier monitoring, flood protection, and affordable climate technology. Its latest climate plan aims to cut projected emissions by 50pc by 2035, with 17 percentage points unconditional and the remaining 33 reliant on international support. This gives Pakistan grounds to seek investment in cleaner energy, transport, and agriculture. But it must also pursue reforms at home, while pressing for stronger global action to reduce emissions.
Pakistan’s preparations for COP31 offer an opportunity to put these priorities into practice. Its planned pavilion sessions in Antalya cover disaster preparedness, solar electrification, local adaptation, and climate investment projects. These discussions should lead to partnerships and investment proposals. Islamabad should identify priority projects and report publicly on commitments secured and money received. Provincial governments must be involved, as irrigation, land use, drainage, and emergency services are largely their responsibility. Local communities should help determine which projects receive priority funding. Pakistan must also address problems that international aid alone cannot solve, including construction on floodplains and poor enforcement of environmental rules. COP31 may produce modest advances rather than a sweeping agreement. But Pakistan can still make progress by presenting workable proposals and showing that the assistance it receives will benefit those most at risk.
Published in Dawn, November 9th, 2026

title: Beyond viewership
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN has an enormous appetite for online content. According to the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority, it leads the world in daily YouTube viewership, with 96m users watching 560m videos a day. TikTok and WhatsApp command similarly vast audiences. And yet millions of Pakistanis struggle with slow connections, patchy mobile coverage, and unreliable service. A video may load eventually, but a student attending a virtual class or a small business processing a payment cannot afford interruptions. The government should, therefore, measure digital progress by whether people can depend on the internet to learn, work, and earn, rather than by the number of accounts opened or videos watched. In smaller towns and rural areas, adequate coverage remains elusive, deepening inequalities between citizens who can access opportunities online and those who cannot. Even in major cities, users complain of poor service. The expansion of 5G to selected cities is welcome, but it means little to those struggling with basic connectivity. Investment in fibre networks, wider coverage, and network maintenance must be matched with affordable packages and meaningful regulatory oversight. Operators should be held to measurable service standards, while arbitrary curbs that disrupt communications and business must end.
Infrastructure alone, however, will not create a digitally capable society. Pakistan’s extraordinary social media consumption tells us little about how confidently its citizens can navigate the online world. Many users remain vulnerable to scams, identity theft, and the misuse of personal information. Others lack the skills to apply digital tools to education and employment. Digital literacy must become a priority, beginning in schools and extending through colleges, vocational institutes, and training centres. Lessons must go beyond operating smartphones to cover online safety, fact-checking, privacy, digital payments, and responsible AI use. Special efforts are needed to reach women, older citizens, and rural populations. Public institutions could work with telecom companies, educators, and civil society to offer practical instruction in local languages. Such programmes would help turn passive consumption into useful participation in the digital economy. Pakistan has no shortage of people willing to go online. What it lacks is a reliable network and a broad base of skills to make that access worthwhile.
Published in Dawn, November 9th, 2026

title: Nuclear arc
author: none@none.com (Huma Yusuf)
content:
LAST week, Iranian state media broadcast instructions on how citizens could stay safe in the event of a nuclear strike. The broadcast covered what people should do if caught in an atomic flash, tips on decontaminating clothes, and what families should keep ready in a ‘nuclear emergency bag’. In the midst of a spiralling regional conflict, this dystopian broadcast is a chilling reminder of how much worse it could get — and so, of how urgently de-escalation is required, particularly as the US and Israel enter a period of political uncertainty following respective elections.
De-escalation efforts are underway, with Qatar reportedly pushing hard for a negotiated end to the conflict. These negotiations hinge on Iran agreeing to reopen its nuclear programme to inspections and accepting curbs on enrichment levels in exchange for US sanctions relief. Such a negotiated end would be very welcome, given how the spectre of nuclear conflict increasingly haunts the Middle East.
One factor that could influence the way this de-escalation proceeds is how the US Congress, freshly stuffed with Democrats, may tackle the US-Saudi civilian nuclear agreement reached this summer. The agreement for civilian nuclear cooperation paves the way for the US transferring technology to Saudi Arabia that would enable it to enrich uranium for nuclear energy production within the kingdom. This would be an exceptional agreement because, as Robert Einhorn points out in a brief for Brookings, Washington typically opposes the spread of fuel-cycle capabilities to new countries.
When announced, the deal rang alarm bells for nuclear non-proliferation experts because it does not require Saudi Arabia to adhere to the IAEA’s Additional Protocol, the legal mechanism which enables the IAEA to check for illicit weapons production. The kingdom refused to sign up to the AP on the basis that potential inspections around holy sites would be too sensitive. This, critics of the deal say, opens a loophole through which Saudi Arabia could divert enriched uranium for weapons production at undeclared sites — an uncomfortable scenario given that Riyadh has stated it would pursue weapons production if Iran acquired nuclear weapons.
The US-Saudi civilian nuclear pact will impact Iran’s strategy.
The Trump administration is willing to proceed with the deal for the following reasons: the civilian nuclear technology transfer will be governed by a Bilateral Safeguards Agreement, which will allow for inspection and monitoring of all declared sites. The US also envisions an exclusive arrangement with Saudi Arabia, meaning the latter would be locked into a ‘black box’ of US-supplied nuclear know-how, technology and equipment, enabling Washington to closely manage Saudi Arabia’s nuclear capability and production. Finally, Washington has reasoned that if it doesn’t reach an agreement with Riyadh, then Moscow or Beijing will instead, and those deals would inevitably have even fewer protections against nuclear weapons proliferation.
The agreement, currently pending with the Congress, would take effect in mid-December if not proactively blocked (an unlikely scenario given congressional priorities, a likely presidential veto of any block, and cross-party appetite to repair ties with Riyadh). But greater Democratic heft may temper the agreement, including renewed efforts to get Saudi Arabia to agree to the AP, limits on the transfer of sensitive enrichment technology, curbs on data sharing, and enhanced reporting on Riyadh’s compliance with non-proliferation terms to Congress.
In all scenarios, the US-Saudi civilian nuclear pact, and the proliferation risks it is perceived to en-
tail, will influe­nce Iran’s app­roach to conflict resolution, pot­e­ntially stymying progress on curtailing Teh­r­an’s nuclear am-bitions. The pro­spect — ho­we-
ver distant — of a nuclear-armed Saudi Arabia in addition to Israel is unlikely to inspire Tehran to disarmament. It will also create regional appetite for more civilian nuclear deals with less adherence to the AP and more localisation of uranium enrichment. Turkey, for example, which has civilian nuclear cooperation deals with the US, Russia, and China, or the UAE, which has an existing agreement with the US that disallows uranium enrichment, may seek technology transfer to enable enrichment and reprocessing within their borders.
What are the security implications of a Middle East with varying degrees of enrichment capabilities subject to different inspections regimes? The idea is concerning, and requires sensible controls and scenario planning to prevent rampant proliferation. Above all, it requires trust among regional actors that civilian nuclear capability will not be repurposed for weapons production. Sadly, the mere potential for proliferation will exacerbate, not ease, the regional trust deficit.
The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.
