title: Climate diagnosis
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE Lancet Countdown’s latest findings should change how Pakistan thinks about illness as much as how it thinks about climate change. The report estimates that heat contributed to 710,000 deaths worldwide in 2023. In Pakistan, a patient arriving at a clinic with dehydration, kidney injury or breathing difficulties may be experiencing the effects of extreme weather without that connection ever entering the medical record. A child treated for diarrhoea after flooding, or an elderly person whose heart condition deteriorates during prolonged heat, becomes another isolated case rather than part of a wider pattern. The result is a dangerous knowledge gap. Without reliable information on where climate-related illnesses occur, who is most affected and how many lives are lost, health authorities cannot judge the scale of the problem. Climate change is already altering the demands placed on medicine; Pakistan’s healthcare planning has yet to catch up.
This is where the warning from former health officials deserves closer attention. Rather than producing another catalogue of vulnerabilities, the government should begin with what hospitals and clinics can actually record, diagnose and treat. Provincial health departments could require major facilities to track heatstroke, dehydration, acute kidney injury and other conditions aggravated by extreme weather, with data reviewed alongside local temperature and rainfall trends. Primary-care staff need practical guidance for recognising heat illness early, especially among children, older people and patients taking medicines that affect hydration. Hospitals should examine whether their emergency departments can cope with seasonal surges, and whether essential treatment can continue when power or water supplies fail. None of this requires waiting for another international declaration. It requires health officials to treat climate exposure as a routine part of patient care. Public reporting would also reveal which districts lack the staff, equipment and referral arrangements to respond. Pakistan has spent years describing itself as vulnerable to climate change. The Lancet findings present a more immediate challenge: can its health system identify the people being harmed, offer them treatment and learn enough from their cases to prevent avoidable deaths?

title: Without consequence
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
JOURNALISTS today face ever more sophisticated threats, while those who target them continue to walk free. From drone attacks to online harassment and legal intimidation, the methods of silencing reporters are multiplying, with little fear of punishment. This year’s International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, observed today, carries the theme ‘Threats Evolve. Impunity Endures’. According to Unesco, 189 journalists were killed in 2024 and 2025, most of them in conflict zones. Yet justice remains elusive in the vast majority of cases. The global impunity rate has risen to 86pc, the first increase since Unesco began measuring it in 2012. This failure to punish those responsible sends a dangerous message: journalists can be attacked or killed without fear of consequence. 
Gaza shows what happens when those responsible are not held to account. The Committee to Protect Journalists recorded 129 journalists killed worldwide in 2025, with Israel responsible for two-thirds of the deaths. In August that year, Israeli strikes on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital killed 22 people, including five journalists. An AP investigation published a year later found that nobody had been held accountable. For Palestinian journalists, who have been reporting a war largely closed to foreign media, the dangers are especially severe. Their deaths leave the outside world with fewer people able to document what is happening. Similarly, in Sudan and Ukraine, journalists risk their lives exposing the horrors of war, while those who target them often escape justice. Without independent investigations and punishment for those found responsible, promises to protect journalists will remain empty.
Pakistan’s record is also deeply troubling. Freedom Network’s latest report documents threats and assaults against journalists, along with 45 cases of legal action or threatened prosecution. The growing use of Peca against journalists investigating official wrongdoing is particularly worrying. Repeated summonses, seized devices and costly court battles are enough to silence a reporter even without a conviction. The human cost of this failure is evident in the case of journalist Mudassar Mahmood Naru. Eight years after his disappearance, his son is growing up without a father and his family is still waiting for answers. The laws meant to protect journalists offer little comfort when the bodies responsible for enforcing them fail to act. In smaller towns, where reporters have fewer resources, intimidation often goes unreported. The state must ensure that attacks are properly investigated, protection bodies function and cybercrime laws are not used to punish legitimate reporting. A country where journalists fear telling the truth more than wrongdoers fear being exposed has its priorities wrong.

title: Medicating a broken system
author: none@none.com (Murad Moosa Khan)
content:
THE psychiatric profession faces a fundamental question: are we treating people’s distress as a problem located inside their minds when much of what troubles them lies outside, in the conditions of their lives? The question has particular urgency in Pakistan, where a recent national survey of more than 17,000 individuals showed that one in three adults suffers from some sort of diagnosable mental disorder. What is leading to this mental health crisis in Pakistan?
The answer may lie in understanding people’s circumstances rather than assigning diagnoses. Unfortunately, we have become so preoccupied with diagnosing and treating individuals that we have lost sight of the social conditions that make them ill.
What does it mean to treat the anxiety of someone whose future is insecure or offer counselling to a man who cannot provide for his family? How far can psychological therapy help a woman who is in constant fear due to unabated domestic violence? Treatment may offer some relief, at least temporarily, but if the circumstances remain unchanged, we risk helping the person endure a problem that society continues to create — and ignore. This is the central limitation of an individualised approach to mental health: it turns a social problem into a personal responsibility.
Pakistan’s mental health discourse focuses on ‘raising awareness, reducing stigma, increasing access to psychological support, early identification, and referral to specialist services’. While these are important, they can become politically convenient substitutes for confronting the structural determinants of psychological distress. Awareness campaigns do not create jobs. Teaching resilience through mental health apps does not increase household incomes. Screening programmes do not stop domestic violence or child sexual abuse. Counselling cannot substitute for social protection, affordable education and health, or protection against violence.
This is the contradiction in Pakistan’s policies: awareness without accountability. This becomes particularly stark when the government acknowledges mental health as a public health priority but does nothing to address the economic and social factors that people face daily. We need to move beyond the narrow thinking that mental health improves when people become more aware of mental illness and more willing to seek treatment. We must also ask why so many people are exposed to toxic conditions that threaten their well-being in the first place.
Improving mental health requires more than treating the consequences of social and economic failure.
Locating distress primarily within individuals obscures questions of power and responsibility. When social adversity is translated into individual diagnoses, ignoring the person’s context, he/she becomes the site of intervention while institutions and governments escape scrutiny. When we teach people resilience we reinforce that the central task is to help people withstand adversity rather than reduce the adversity itself. In Pakistan, marked by profound inequalities, it turns psychiatry, however unintentionally, into an instrument of adaptation to injustice.
Instead, we should ask: what has happened to this person, and what continues to make their life difficult? Mental health assessments should explore not only symptoms and psychiatric history but also employment, debt, housing, family relationships, violence, etc. It is important to understand the person’s own explanation of their distress rather than assuming that a diagnostic label of ‘depression’ or ‘anxiety’ provides the complete account.
This approach does not eliminate diagnosis or medication. Those experiencing severe symptoms should have access to evidence-based treatment. The distinction is between using biomedical interventions when indicated and treating the biomedical explanation as sufficient in every case. The approach also has important policy implications. Pakistan has a good record of developing policies but an extremely poor one for implementing them. There is no reason to be optimistic that the recently launched National Mental Health Policy will not meet the same fate. It is futile to talk about a mental health policy without integrating social determinants into planning and also having a clear strategy for their implementation. The federal and provincial governments must be held accountable for how they will do so.
Mental health programmes must be evaluated against outcomes that matter in people’s lives, not simply symptom improvement. Mental health professionals and institutions must engage with the political and economic conditions shaping their patients’ lives. It requires them to recognise that suffering has social causes and that their professional obligations do not end at the clinic door. They must be willing to speak truth to power and not simply have their photographs taken with government officials and political leaders.
Pakistan does not face a choice between treating mental illness and addressing poverty, inequality, or violence. It needs both. The mistake is investing in the former while neglecting the latter. A diagnosis is never a complete explanation, and an effective treatment plan must take into account people’s circumstances. How ethical is it to ask people to become more resilient to bear conditions that public policy could make less damaging or ask people to practise relaxation exercises while their livelihoods collapse, to cultivate optimism while their prospects disappear, or to dev­elop coping skills while they remain exposed to violence? Such interventions may provide relief, but they cannot substitute for social justice.
Pakistan’s mental health crisis cannot be addressed solely through more psychiatrists, better access to mental health services (which are poorly organised anyway), more prescriptions, more awareness campaigns, or more screening. These are necessary components of care, but they cannot compensate for policies that perpetuate insecurity and exclusion. Improving mental health requires more than treating the consequences of social and economic failure. It requires taking responsibility for the conditions that produce them.
A society committed to mental well-being must do more than teach people how to endure their circumstances. It must also work to make those circumstances more bearable. 
The writer is professor emeritus of psychiatry at Aga Khan University.

title: Fighting harassment
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
WORKPLACE harassment is often narrowly defined as sexual misconduct. A resolution passed by the National Assembly on Friday puts such notions to rest. Reaffirming parliament’s commitment towards safeguarding an individual’s dignity and rights, it asserts that harassment extends beyond sexual advances. The inclusion of intimidation, misuse of authority, and gender-based humiliation completes the definition. The Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 supports the view: “Any unwelcome sexual advance, request … sexually demeaning attitudes, causing interference with work performance or creating an intimidating, hostile or offensive work environment, or the attempt to punish the complainant. …”  Power derived from gender or position drives all forms of harassment. Yet, Pakistan’s failure to enforce legal deterrents continues to create more silent victims.
Those who exploit have for too long escaped penalties due to procedural loopholes. The Women’s Parliamentary Caucus would do well to address the necessity of accountability processes within organisations. Laws will remain mere formalities until the state devises monitoring mechanisms to ensure both managements and the criminal justice system do not falter in delivering justice. Human rights defenders have not only raised concern about the shoddy application of the harassment law but also highlighted how lack of proper penalisation has economic consequences. It jeopardises productivity as hostile workplaces force women out of the workforce.First,all stakeholders must treat an employee and a workplace in a wider sense to include informal areas and workers — sportspersons, artists, domestic workers, students, and others. Second, employers should face tougher action — hefty fines, suspension and even removal from office. Additionally, training, awareness and surveillance are as significant as transparent and accessible complaint systems. Lastly, the meaning of workplace harassment does not change if it occurs outside the confines of a work setting.
Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

title: A might-is-right world
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
THE world is passing through one of the most volatile periods in modern history. It is more unstable today than at any time since the end of the Cold War. The international system is fragmenting with rising big-power tensions. The old order with whatever rules it had is gone. 
Power shifts continue to reshape the international landscape, marking the advent of a multipolar era. The disregard for international law and norms by big and regional powers has left countries having to navigate a rule-less terrain at a time of great uncertainty. Hard power has made a comeback. Powerful countries and regional powers are using military force or other coercive instruments to try to bend other states to their will. The threat or the use of force has become an option of first and not last resort, and the means to prevail over others. These actions defy international law and global norms but continue with impunity. Diplomacy only happens after missiles have been fired.
Conflicts proliferate across the world — two major wars, between the US-Israel and Iran and between Ukraine and Russia as well as Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza and military actions against its neighbours. There are a record number of conflicts today. A study by a Swedish university has counted the highest number of conflicts between states in 2025 since World War II. There are 65 active conflicts according to its data for last year. The risk of a global conflagration is also heightening.  Can this push the world to the brink of a third world war? A new book seeks to answer this frequently raised question. War is Interested in You: The Breakdown of International Order and the Threat of World War Three by distinguished British columnist Gideon Rachman is an insightful book on a subject that is especially relevant today. He borrows the book’s title from Trotsky: “You may not be interested in war, but war is interested in you” — meaning war will come whether anyone wants it or is thinking about it. Rachman identifies three fundamental reasons for the surge in conflicts and breakdown of international order. The first is the shifting global balance of power which is challenging US dominance. The second is the rise of what he calls ‘strongmen leaders’ who regard war as a necessary and legitimate tool to achieve their ends. The third is a consequence of the first two; as these trends take hold international rules and law are breaking down. “A law-governed world is giving way to a might-makes-right world,” he writes.  
In explaining these causal factors, Rachman argues that the relative decline of the Western alliance and America’s retrenchment from its global role created an “opening” for “revisionist” powers dissatisfied with the present world order to take more risks. He cites Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and China’s more aggressive posture on Taiwan as cases in point. Trump’s use of military force against Iran, in defiance of international law and ignoring the views of its allies, has further contributed to the collapse of global order.  
Can distinct regional conflicts merge to push the world to the brink of a third world war?
Greater international insecurity also stems from the emergence of a new generation of self-styled strongman leaders — Putin, Trump, Netanyahu — who deride the idea of a rules-based international order. Their acceptance of territorial annexation and belief in ‘might-makes-right’ has heightened the risk of international conflict. Rachman suggests that both Trump and Putin subscribe to the “spheres of influence” theory, which they see as a more reliable guarantor of peace and stability than a rules-based order. The starkest expression of this, he asserts, is Trump’s revival of the Monroe doctrine for the Western Hemisphere.  
In what Rachman characterises as a “might is right” world, growing global insecurity is driving up defence spending. Global rules and international institutions are being upended by strongman leaders, increasing the risk of more wars. While acts of war are the most dramatic examples of the breakdown of the rules-based order, Rachman argues that international institutions are crumbling in other ways too. Trump’s trade war and protectionist policies are, for example, accelerating this erosion.  
Rachman examines today’s major wars and argues that while they have been distinct regional conflicts, they intersect at various points. But as these separate conflicts escalate, they risk eventually merging. His concept of an ‘axis of adversaries’ of the West or ‘axis of upheaval’ challenging the US-led world order greatly exaggerates the degree of cooperation between Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran whose interests are hardly identical. They may all want an end to US hegemony but that doesn’t make them partners in an alliance acting in unison. The argument does not stand up to scrutiny. Rachman is unable to convincingly establish the “practical and ideological” links he posits between them. In fact, he himself acknowledges the limits of the Russian-Chinese partnership and strains among the four countries.
To the question of whether a conflict-ridden world is heading towards a global conflagration, Rachman’s answer is carefully qualified. A world war, he argues, would have two defining characteristics. One, the world’s major powers would have to be in direct conflict as they were in the First and Second World Wars. Two, the conflict would have to span continents. These conditions do not obtain today but they cannot be ruled out in the future.He sees a direct conflict between the US and China as the greatest risk. 
Rachman devotes a chapter to last year’s conflict between India and Pakistan. It adds little to what has already been written about the military confrontation between the two nuclear neighbours. He sees the four-day conflict in May 2025 as a serious setback to India’s ambitions and efforts to de-hyphenate from Pakistan. Among the lessons he draws from this episode is that “the risks of a very dangerous conflict in South Asia get too little attention compared to other global trouble spots”. He argues that the risk of future conflicts is heightened by the fact that both countries deployed increasingly sophisticated weapons during the crisis.
This is an intelligent book well worth reading for its sharp perspectives on war and peace even if one might disagree with some of the author’s assertions. 
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

title: Uncertain local governments
author: none@none.com (Ahmed Bilal Mehboob)
content:
THE battle between the Election Commission of Pakistan and the provincial and federal governments has been an almost permanent feature of Pakistan’s electoral scene since 2010, when the responsibility for holding local government elections was entrusted to the Commission under the 18th Amendment. Currently, the ECP is fighting a four-way battle — with the provincial governments of Punjab and KP, the federal government, and the cantonment boards — for LG elections in the two provinces, Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT), and the cantonment boards. The LGs in Sindh and Balochistan (except in the largest district of Quetta, where the entire term passed without election) have yet to complete their terms.
The ICT LG election is the most disappointing case. The last LG election in ICT was held in November 2015. Its five-year term ended on Feb 14, 2021. Under the Elections Act, 2017, the new election was to take place within 120 days after the previous LGs’ term ended, making June 15, 2021, the due date for the next election. For more than five years, the ECP and the federal government have been haggling over legal points and the possible date of the next election. Since 2021, the ECP has issued the election schedule four times and carried out fresh delimitation five times. Each time it has had to eat humble pie by withdrawing the schedule as the federal government changed the goalposts and amended the LG election law. The latest in the series was the ICT Local Government (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, promulgated on Jan 10, 2026, which drastically changed the capital’s LG system. However, the ordinance lapsed in September 2026.
While parliament is going through the motions of converting the lapsed ordinance into an act of parliament, the ECP maintains that the old ICTLGA, 2015, stands resurrected after the ordinance lapsed and, therefore, issued a polling schedule on Oct 25, fixing Dec 20 as polling day. Looking back at the federal government’s track record, the new act is likely to pass in the next few days, after which the ECP would have no choice but to withdraw the schedule and begin preparations anew.
The case of KP is not very different; the terms of the LGs expired on June 19, 2026, after which new elections should have taken place by Oct 20, but the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local Government (Amendment) Act, 2026,was passedand became effective on July 16 this year. It changed the size of the village and neighbourhood councils. The ECP strongly objected to the amendment, termed it a delaying tactic, and asked the provincial government to review the law. In the meantime, the ECP is proceeding with preparations to hold the LG polls, except in 12 districts where the law and order situation doesn’t permit polls. The ECP has yet to issue an election schedule. Still, it remains to be seen whether the National Assembly, which has the legislative powers of the KP Assembly after the proclamation of emergency, will amend the LG law or whether the elections will be postponed yet again on some pretext or the other.
The ECP is battling both the federal and provincial governments that are reluctant to hold LG polls.
All formalities for holding the LG election in Punjab have been completed by the ECP and the Punjab government under the Punjab Local Government Act, 2025. If finally held, this will be the first LG election in roughly 11 years. The election was supposed to be held in May 2022, but a series of new laws and amendments kept postponing it. Although the Punjab government ministerial committee and the ECP agreed to hold the election in three phases between Dec 15 and Jan 15, the Punjab government changed its mind and asked the ECP to defer the election until April 2027 because of dense fog and school exams in December. The ECP immediately rejected the new dates and asked its secretariat to prepare an election schedule based on the earlier agreed dates. The election schedule has not yet been issued; one should wait to see which side blinks first.
The election to 43 cantonment boards in the country was due on Aug 8 as the four-year term of the previously elected boards expired on April 11, 2026. The cantonment boards’ election has an additional prerequisite: the ECP should receive the federal government’s request before holding the election. Reportedly, no such request has been received, and the ECP, given the legal requirement to hold elections within 120 days of the expiry of the term, is trying to reach out to the federal government. Regardless of the outcome of these efforts, the election to the cantonment boards is also overdue.
These four stories lead to a single conclusion: both the federal and provincial governments are reluctant to hold LG elections on one pretext or another. The key flaw in the system is that while the ECP is responsible for holding LG elections, the governments and their legislatures alone write the LG laws. There is no bar on legislatures amending LG laws. As demonstrated repeatedly, the law can be amended after the announcement of the election schedule and even a few days before polling day, undoing all the preparation made by the ECP such as delimiting LG boundaries. The solution is for parliament to amend the Elections Act, 2017, and bar any amendment to the LG laws after the expiry of the LG term, so the ECP can prepare unimpeded and hold timely elections. 
As if these difficulties were not enough to make the future of LGs uncertain, another layer of unpredictability has been added by the possibility of carving out new provinces and, in the case of ICT, by the announcement that Islamabad may soon have provincial status. This may give the government yet another pretext to slow-walk LG elections. 
The writer is the president of Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.president@pildat.org

title: ‘L’état, c’est moi’
author: none@none.com (Asad-ul-Mulk)
content:
THE insertion of Article 172(3) in Pakistan’s Constitution via the 18th Amendment was stupendously transformative, as it restructured the sovereign ownership of oil and gas. In the new constitutional scheme, the federation and the provinces were to be co-owners of oil and gas produced within the provinces. Yet, even after 16 years, the full benefits of this constitutionally bestowed co-ownership remain a covenant to be realised for the provinces.
Around the time John D. Rockefeller was tapping into the Pennsylvania oil fields, India enacted its first oil legislation, the Petroleum Act, 1881. The legislation did not address ownership; rather, it regulated only the import, transportation, and possession of oil. The concept of private ownership of oil and gas resources, prevalent in the US and recognised by its supreme court as early as ‘Brown vs Spilman’ (1895), would never see the light of day in the Indian subcontinent; instead, de facto sovereign control would reign.
The Indian Councils Acts, 1892 and 1909, and the Government of India Acts, 1915 and 1919,allowed the ‘central government’ to regulate oil, though they were gleefully silent on ownership. The Petroleum Act, 1934,did not rework this much. In any event, before the Government of India Act, 1935, the government of India was unitary and only thereafter became federal, listing ‘oil’ as a federal subject.
This position persisted under Pakistan’s constitutions of 1956, 1962, and 1973, with ‘gas’ additionally listed as a federal subject. The 18th Amendment altered this legal paradigm by introducing Article 172(3), which proclaims: “Subject to the existing commitments and obligations, mineral oil, and natural gas within the province or the territorial waters adjacent thereto shall vest jointly and equally in that province and the federal government.”
Cooperative federalism in the matter of oil and gas is being undermined.
Though by virtue of Article 97 and 137 of the Constitution, the federal government retains executive authority over the regulation of oil and gas, the doctrine of ‘joint ownership’, together with oil and gas appearing in the Federal Legislative List, Part-II, means that the Council of Common Interests (CCI), by virtue of Article 154 of the Constitution, is empowered to formulate and regulate policies in respect thereof, and exercise supervision and control over related institutions.
Clause 1.3.6 of the Petroleum Policy, 2012, enacted by the CCI, establishes a “reorganised Directorate General of Petroleum Concessions (DGPC) comprising federal and provincial representatives”. The de jure responsibility of the reorganised DGPC, inter alia, is to “decide the matters of grants, regulation, annulment and monitoring of all petroleum concessions” in the country, consistent with the Petroleum Rules, 2013.
Regrettably, the provincial directors who are part of the reorganised DGPC have been given no de facto say in matters of “grants, regulations and annulments” of petroleum rights. The federal director at the reorganised DGPC deals with such matters unilaterally, recognising no situation where he can legally be outvoted, even by the four provincial directors combined.
This approach is akin to Louis XIV of France declaring before the Parliament of Paris in 1655: “l’état, c’est moi” (“the state — it’s me”). The federal director, being a state functionary and one member out of a total of five who form the reorganised DGPC, cannot single-handedly claim to be the reorganised DGPC (though he does so and this ingression is less a personal trait, and more a projection of the federal government’s resolve to maintain its hegemony over oil and gas resources, even when the Constitution says otherwise).
In ‘Wattan Party vs Fede­ration of Pakistan’ (2006), the Supreme Court held CCI policies enacted under Article 154 to be binding on the federal government. Thus, if the latter takes exception to the implementation of a particular provision of the Petroleum Policy, 2012, vis-à-vis the role of the reorganised DGPC, then its remedy lies in referring the matter to a joint sitting of parliament in accordance with Article 154(7), and not in flouting the same.
“The earth, and all that is therein, is given to men, for the support and comfort of their being. Yet being given for the use of men, there must of necessity be a means to appropriate them some way,” wrote John Locke in his Second Treatise of Government. The Constitution of Pakistan prescribes appropriation, which attends to the ownership, regulation, and control of oil and gas resources in a spirit of cooperative federalism. Yet the federal government’s functionaries can scarcely resist bellowing to their provincial counterparts, ‘l’etat, c’est moi’. 
The writer is a practising barrister.

summary: The 18th Amendment, through Article 172(3), fundamentally transformed oil and gas ownership by establishing joint and equal vesting in provinces and the federal government.

Despite constitutional provisions for cooperative federalism, the full benefits of co-ownership for provinces remain unrealized due to the federal government's continued hegemonic control over resource regulation.

Historically, oil and gas ownership in the subcontinent was under de facto sovereign control, with 'oil' becoming a federal subject only after the Government of India Act, 1935, a position maintained until the 18th Amendment.

The federal government's functionaries, specifically the federal director at the reorganised DGPC, unilaterally manage petroleum concessions, effectively flouting the spirit of the Petroleum Policy, 2012, and the Supreme Court's directives on CCI policies.

The Petroleum Policy, 2012, enacted by the Council of Common Interests (CCI), established a reorganised Directorate General of Petroleum Concessions (DGPC) with federal and provincial representatives.
The Supreme Court case 'Wattan Party vs Federation of Pakistan' (2006) held that policies enacted by the CCI under Article 154 are binding on the federal government.

title: Cost of provinces
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE cost would be steep. We all knew that. An Islamabad-based think tank has now put figures to those costs. That gives a fiscal dimension to a debate that has largely been driven by political demands and promises of better administration.
The Policy Research Institute of Market Economy estimates that creating two more provinces in Punjab could add Rs47bn to Rs57bn to annual recurring expenditure. The bill could rise to Rs610bn-Rs730bn if all the country’s 30 divisional units were turned into provinces.
Every new province would require a permanent administrative and political structure, including a governor, chief minister, assembly, secretariat and high court. Their salaries, operating expenses and overheads would have to be met year after year, leaving less money for development.
The figures expose a major weakness in the argument for creating more provinces: political and administrative restructuring is often presented as an inexpensive way to make government more responsive. It is not.
    
Smaller administrative units create another layer of government whose costs would be hard to justify. If a substantial portion of their allocations goes towards maintaining political and administrative establishments, little would remain for schools, hospitals and other essential services. Citizens promised better governance could end up paying for an expensive new tier without seeing much improvement.
There is, of course, a real case for reorganising provincial boundaries.
Punjab’s size and population, regional disparities and the sense of political and economic neglect in its southern districts cannot be dismissed. The demand for a separate South Punjab province reflects genuine grievances over unequal development. But these grievances cannot be resolved simply by creating new capitals, assemblies and secretariats. Nor should the fiscal argument be used to brush aside legitimate demands for political representation and administrative autonomy.
    
Can the same objectives be achieved through empowered local governments?
Political parties’ record of repeatedly suspending, delaying or weakening elected LGs suggests that the problem is less the size of provinces than the reluctance of political leadership to devolve power and resources.
Functional LGs, with predictable funding, elected representatives and clearly defined responsibilities, could take decision-making nearer to citizens without multiplying provincial overheads.
Any proposal for provincial restructuring must show how it would improve public services. It must also establish how new units would finance recurring expenditure. The creation of provinces is a long-term fiscal and constitutional commitment. Political parties demanding new provinces must explain how they intend to pay for them and what improvements citizens can expect.
Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

title: India’s water blackmail
author: none@none.com (Khurram Abbas)
content:
SINCE April 2025, when India unilaterally suspended the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), most scholarship has treated it as a political decision by the BJP-led NDA government. While it is true that the BJP has been developing a narrative that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi was ‘rectifying’ the ‘mistakes’ of the Nehruvian era, the decisions and developments during the past 18 months suggest that New Delhi is developing a long-term strategy to strangle Pakistan economically.
India’s primary target in this strategic campaign is the Chenab river, which it is systematically converting into a long-term instrument of leverage to dictate Pakistan’s foreign policy, weaken its stance on Kashmir, and dominate bilateral relations. In the 18 months since it decided to keep the IWT in abeyance, India has aggressively leveraged this treaty vacuum to build a massive network of storage, regulation, and diversion infrastructure on the Chenab. New and accelerated hydroelectric power projects, primarily concentrated in the Chenab basin, have ballooned from a baseline capacity of 3,263 MW to 7,620.5 MW, supported by a massive financial outlay of approximately Indian rupees 414.04 billion.
No single dam or diversion canal can permanently dry up a river. However, a highly synchronised, connected network of mega structures, coupled with diversion canals, can fundamentally determine who controls the timing and volume of river flow. India is trying to apply a two-pronged strategy, ie, increase storage capacity and enhance the ability to divert the Chenab’s water. India’s strategic roadmap involves five megaprojects alongside extensive local diversions. This includes Sawalkot (1,856 MW), Kirthai I & II (1,320 MW), Pakal Dul (1,000 MW), Ratle (850 MW), and Bursar Storage (800 MW).
India’s infrastructure push began in May 2025, with the announcement of the tender for the Uri-II project (240 MW), followed quickly in June 2025 by the tender announcement for the Dulhasti-II project (260 MW). Activity accelerated in July 2025 with two major announcements — first, a tender for the removal of deposited sediments from the Salal Dam Reservoir, and second, the Sawalkot project (1,856 MW) tender under international competitive bidding. In March 2026, civil contracts were officially awarded for both the Uri-I stage II and Dulhasti stage-II projects, alongside the official tender announcement for the highly controversial Chenab-Beas Link Tunnel Project (Link-3). These aforementioned projects command a combined potential diversion and storage capacity of roughly 7.287 MAF.
For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic foundations.
The Chenab-Beas Link Project is particularly consequential. With a reported budget of Indian rupees 23.52bn, it proposes to transfer water from the Chandra river, a major Chenab tributary, through an 8.7-kilometre tunnel into the Beas basin and onward through a 113km canal network to eastern Indian states. The proposed diversion of 1.9 MAF annually from the Chenab basin raises serious questions about compliance with Article III of the IWT.
The threat of manipulation, or the Chenab’s vulnerabilities, poses a direct risk to Pakistan’s economic survival, social stability, and national security. The Chenab directly irrigates agricultural lands across more than 11 districts of central Punjab, the country’s undisputed food basket. These districts form the densest core of the famous rice-wheat cropping zone. This 11-district area accounts for about 22 to 25 per cent of Pakistan’s national food grain output. If India controls water flows during October to December or May to July, it may affect seasonal yields in this zone. In such a scenario, it could cause a direct blow of $9bn to $11bn to Pakistan’s economy.
The broader impact would ripple through the national economy in several ways. Pakistan would be forced to spend billions of scarce foreign exchange reserves to import basic food commodities. Instead of generating $3.3bn to $4bn from booming rice exports, the country would face a multibillion-dollar trade deficit just trying to secure alternative grain imports. Second, any sustained restriction on, or unpredictable disruption to, these water flows would threaten the livelihoods of millions of farming households, while endangering crops and compromising national food security.
Therefore, Islamabad must view India’s decision to place the IWT in abeyance as another dimension of New Delhi’s long-standing and coordinated policy of economic strangulation of Pakistan. For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic foundations. New Delhi has been consistently trying to restrict Islamabad’s access to global capital and limit its trade capacity. A primary example is India’s aggressive lobbying within the Financial Action Task Force, where it has consistently tried to politicise technical compliance and block Pakistan’s removal from the grey list to discourage foreign direct investment and cripple its banking sector. Beyond regulatory warfare, India has systematically disrupted regional trade platforms, such as Saarc, effectively stalling economic integration across South Asia to keep Pakistan regionally isolated.
Faced with this asymmetric threat, Islamabad’s response has been largely concentrated on the external front. Pakistan’s state apparatus has consistently pursued international legal and diplomatic channels. However, a dangerous policy gap exists on the domestic front. Ground-level preparedness is profoundly lacking. The agrarian communities, provincial irrigation departments, and economic sectors that will bear the immediate impact of India’s upstream infrastructure remain highly vulnerable. Pakistan lacks the modern water-storage infrastructure, optimised canal lining, crop-switching strategies, and real-time early warning systems needed to survive sudden changes in river flows.
Hence, Islamabad should complement its legal and diplomatic efforts with urgent domestic reforms. Pakistan must declare a national water emergency, educate vulnerable communities in 11 districts of central Punjab that depend on the Chenab, expedite dam construction, and modernise irrigation. Without urgent preparedness, Islamabad will risk surrendering its agricultural security to Delhi’s water blackmail. 
The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.
Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

title: Off the back seat
author: none@none.com (Muna Khan)
content:
SOME time in the mid-2000s, I attended a conference for journalists in Goa. I remember very little of the panels. What I remember is going into town. Women everywhere, on scooters. Young women in jeans. Middle-aged women in saris, the pallu tucked in, a shopping bag on the footboard. Older women with grey buns and sensible sandals, weaving through traffic as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world. Because it was.
I kept staring. Nobody else did.
This was next door. Same subcontinent, same heat, same chaotic roads, same aunties. So why was it unthinkable at home? In Karachi, a woman on a motorbike belonged on the back seat, perched sideways, dupatta wrapped tight so it would not catch in the wheel, one hand gripping the seat and the other holding a child. She was a passenger, in every sense. I never expected to see that change in my lifetime.
Last month, a Gallup & Gilani survey found that 83 per cent of Pakistanis believe more women ride two-wheelers today than three years ago. In cities, the figure rises to 91pc. That is perception, not a headcount. But perception matters. People are noticing because there is something to notice.
When the Sindh government launched its Pink Scooty scheme last year, offering free electric scooters to female students and working women, it hit an awkward problem. Only 154 women across the entire province reportedly held motorcycle driving licences in June. You cannot hand a scooter to a woman who is not legally allowed to ride it. So the scheme required a licence and offered free training to get one. Minister Sharjeel Memon told local media that over 50,000 women had applied for licences. From 154 to 50,000. Even allowing for a politician’s optimism, that is not a trend. That is a door swinging open.
Consider the choices before a young woman with a job offer across town.
It did not happen overnight. Karachi’s Women on Wheels programme, launched in 2019, recorded more than 3,000 registrations and trained hundreds of women to ride on the University of Karachi campus. The groundwork was laid quietly, by women willing to wobble, fall, and get back on.
Why does this matter so much? Because in Pakistan, the road to a job runs through the question of how a woman gets there.
Pakistan has one of the lowest rates of female labour force participation in the world. The World Economic Forum puts it at about 28pc. In our cities, World Bank research suggests it has hovered around 10pc for two decades. There are many reasons. Social norms. Childcare. Workplace harassment. But again and again, studies return to the same plain obstacle: transport.
Consider the choices before a young woman in Karachi with a job offer across town. A rickshaw eats into her salary every single day. Ride-hailing costs even more. The bus is crowded, unpredictable, and, too often, a gauntlet of stares and hands. If no brother, father, or husband is free to drive her, the job may simply not be worth taking. A whole career can be lost to the problem of the commute.
A scooter changes that arithmetic. It is cheap to run, cheaper still when it is electric. It goes where buses do not. It leaves when she is ready, not when someone else is. It turns a job across town from a family negotiation into a decision she can make herself.
That is what economic independence looks like on the ground. Not a slogan, but a set of keys.
And independence is the point. For most women, freedom is not an abstraction. It is the ability to earn, spend, leave, and ret­urn on their own ter­ms. Fin­a­ncial freedom is freedom. A woman who can get herself to work can pay her own fees, support her par­ents, save for her children, and, if she must, walk away from a home that is hurting her.
None of this is finished. Being seen is not the same as being accepted. Women riders still face harassment and disapproval. The change is clearer among urban, middle-class women than in villages. And reminders of how far we still have to go. In June, the minister told the Sindh Assembly that traffic police had been instructed to stop men riding the pink scooters after complaints that some women’s brothers had taken them over.
I laughed when I read that. Then I stopped laughing. It says everything about who has usually held the keys in our homes.
But the keys are changing hands. Slowly, unevenly, one licence at a time.
The other day, at a traffic signal, a young woman pulled up beside me on a scooter. Nobody stared. I did, for a moment. Then I smiled. When the light turned green, she was gone. It looked like Goa. It looked normal. It looked like home. 
The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.

title: Exchange hack
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
ON Thursday, the largest cryptocurrency heist in history saw some $6.3bn drained from exchange platform Binance’s own wallets. Most of the funds were moved out in about 20 minutes. The hack dwarfed the previous record, of some $1.5bn from rival exchange Bybit in February 2025. Binance’s own investigation initially suggested that the laptop of one of its engineers had been compromised, which allowed attackers to gain access to an internal service used to submit withdrawals. It later emerged that this had been a sophisticated attack involving multiple breach points in Binance’s systems, malicious software that covered its tracks as it operated, and abuse of a feature of the Ethereum network to bypass the exchange’s normal approval controls. Blockchain analytics firms have attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking group. Binance, the largest crypto exchange in the world, has suspended withdrawals as it reviews security.
Though Binance has said it will cover all user losses, news of this incident has shaken the crypto sphere. It also raises serious questions — about custody standards, licensing conditions for exchanges, and who bears the losses when things go wrong — for countries in the process of embracing cryptocurrency, including Pakistan. The fact is that Binance is considerably more experienced in the crypto trade than most new entrants and regulators. If its security and operational controls can be compromised, then potentially anyone can be at risk. Until early last year, Pakistan treated crypto as a regulatory no-go area. The authorities have since reversed gear. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao has served as a strategic adviser to the Pakistan Crypto Council since April 2025, and in December 2025 the finance ministry signed an MoU with Binance to explore tokenising up to $2bn in sovereign assets. The exchange’s troubles are therefore of direct concern to Islamabad. But though embracing technology is understandable and perhaps also commendable, policymakers must ensure that the risks that come with dealing in crypto are also being actively assessed and addressed. This incident is a timely reminder that the cost of a security failure can be immense. The authorities need to understand what they are getting into, and make provisions to mitigate risk.

title: Cyber safety
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
WHILE the state’s proposal to create a Cybersecurity and Social Media Awareness Council envisages needed interventions to protect children from online harm, the same body’s focus on ‘fake news’ — as described by the government — is cause for concern.
Speaking at a recent seminar in Islamabad, the federal information minister said there is a need to raise awareness about the “dangers of fake news”, while also emphasising the need for digital education in schools and colleges. In particular, he said children should be protected from cyberattacks. At the same event, the IT minister observed that it was important for both parents and children to know who the latter were interacting with online.
There can be little argument with the fact that cyberspace can be a dangerous place for children. According to a Unicef report, one in 16 children in Pakistan aged 12-17 experienced “at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse” in a single year. This comes to around 1.5m children.
Moreover, the National Commission on the Rights of the Child points out that youngsters are vulnerable to “cyberbullying, online grooming, sharing of sexual abuse materials” and other types of harm. There have been disturbing recent reports of even parents and guardians involved in the online abuse of children. It is, therefore, essential to protect youngsters from online predators through digital literacy, while bringing those involved in these abominable crimes to justice. Pakistan’s children face enough challenges; the state must do all it can to protect them from online harm.
But combining steps against cyberbullying and online abuse of children with the state’s campaign against ‘fake news’ needs to be reconsidered. The state of freedom of expression in Pakistan is already quite poor, so any further attempts to clamp down on free speech must be resisted. Instead, the proposed council should focus on protecting children from dangers in the cyber realm, as well as keeping citizens overall safe from online threats.

title: Unsafe blood transfusions
author: none@none.com (Zafar Mirza)
content:
“BLOOD transfusions (48pc) and contaminated needle use (48pc) are the primary contributors to the outbreak.”
This was the conclusion of a joint mission by the Punjab government, WHO, Unicef and UNAIDS investigating the HIV outbreak among children in Taunsa, Dera Ghazi Khan. Between Dec 2024 and April 2025, 120 children under 12 were infected. As unsafe practices continued, the number eventually reached 331, by the time the BBC made its incriminating documentary.
How many more outbreaks will it take before we recognise that this is not an isolated medical mishap but a systemic governance failure?
Pakistan has one of the fastest-growing HIV epidemics in Asia and the world’s largest burden of hepatitis C. Both are blood-borne infections. Unsafe transfusions and contaminated injections are preventable sources of infection, yet they continue to endanger lives, particularly those of poor children who depend on an inadequately regulated healthcare system.
Unsafe blood flows through non-functional institutions.
The tragedy is not that Pakistan lacks the knowledge to make blood transfusions safe. It is that we repeatedly fail to translate policies, technical knowledge and institutional arrangements into action.
Consider history. Established in 2010 with substantial German financial and technical assistance, the Safe Blood Transfusion Programme (SBTP) made important progress. It established 17 state-of-the-art Regional Blood Centres (RBCs) and upgraded and linked 83 public-sector hospital blood banks. It also supported relevant policies, legislation, technical guidelines, training and monitoring systems.
Yet the programme gradually became dormant. After its national coordinator retired in 2020, no replacement was appointed, to date. The programme lost momentum, and opportunities to sustain international cooperation were not adequately pursued. A national initiative that had laid the foundations of reform was left high and dry, without the leadership needed to carry it forward.
This is a familiar Pakistani story: programmes are launched, institutions established, laws enacted and policies approved. Then positions remain vacant, resources are withheld, regulations unfinished and accountability absent.
The consequences are visible nationwide. Islamabad’s Blood Transfusion Authority is non-functional, while its RBC remained inoperative for years before being handed over to the Indus Hospital & Health Network in July 2026. Punjab has yet to frame rules under its 2016 law. Sindh has failed to replace outdated rules despite subsequent legislation. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has a regulatory framework, but its regional centres remain underutilised. Balochistan has laws and institutions, but lacks adequate operational capacity, staffing and financing.
In Aug 2026, a Technical Working Group (TWG) was established following the prime minister’s intervention after the Taunsa outbreak. Its mandate is to translate the earlier task force’s recommendations into action, also reflected in the National Blood Transfusion and Blood Products Policy 2025-2030. The TWG reports directly to the PM monthly.
The TWG’s Sept 2026 policy brief provides a practical roadmap. Its value lies not in announcing another policy but in specifying actions that must be implemented immediately.
First, the SBTP must be revived, with a merit-based, qualified national coordinator, professional staff, a functioning office and adequate resources. The centre must ensure sustainable financing through the recurrent budget and seek renewed international cooperation.
Second, regulatory authorities must become functional. Islamabad needs an operational authority with competent staff and adequate funding. Punjab must frame rules under its existing law and strengthen its authority. Sindh must finalise regulations and build institutional capacity. KP and Balochistan need effective provincial counterparts to the national programme.
Third, RBCs must be linked to hospital blood banks across the public and private sectors. Existing centres are underutilised. Connecting more hospitals would expand access to quality-assured blood and reduce fragmentation. Blood safety cannot be confined to government hospitals while private establishments escape effective regulation.
Fourth, screening standards must be enforced uniformly. The TWG recommends automated chemiluminescence immunoassay as the minimum screening standard, with nucleic acid testing introduced as an additional safeguard. Manual rapid diagnostic kits must be prohibited for donor screening. A real-time national database, including a donor deferral registry, should prevent people with reactive screening results from donating blood again.
Fifth, the Inter-Ministerial Health and Population Council should regularly review blood safety and monitor implementation. Model regulations should be approved by the National Technical Advisory Committee and adopted by provincial authorities.
Finally, Pakistan should reduce its dependence on imported plasma-derived medicinal products. While these products are imported at considerable cost, recovered plasma is wasted or discarded. The TWG recommends a national plasma fractionation programme, with WHO technical assistance, to improve availability and move towards domestic production.
The roadmap is clear. What remains uncertain is whether political will, administrative discipline and financial commitment will be sustained long enough to implement it.
The PM’s direct involvement offers an opportunity, but personal intervention cannot substitute for strong institutions. The real test is whether competent professionals are appointed, funds released, regulations enforced, hospitals connected to safe blood supplies and results independently monitored.
Nor can governments act alone. Citizens, professional associations, medical practitioners, civil society and the media must demand safe healthcare and hold public and private providers accountable. Voluntary, non-remunerated blood donation must be encouraged while infection prevention and control guidelines must be implemented.
The children of Taunsa have already paid an unacceptable price for our collective failure. Their suffering must not become another forgotten episode in Pakistan’s public health history.
The choice is stark: continue treating each outbreak as a temporary media scandal, or confront the institutional weaknesses that make the next one possible. Unsafe blood flows through non-functional institutions.
The writer is a former SAPM on health with ministerial status, adjunct professor of health systems and president of the Pakistan Association of Lifestyle Medicine.

title: What a child drinks
author: none@none.com (Mian Muhammad Junaid)
content:
AT the recent Act for Nutrition Conf­e­rence in Islamabad, organised by DawnMedia, where I joined a panel examining the link between poor water, sanitation and child stunting, much of the discussion was rightly about food: what children eat, how mothers are supported, and why so many families still struggle to access a nutritious diet.
But sitting on that panel, I kept returning to another part of the stunting story that receives far less attention: what is the child drinking?
What happens when the water available at home is unsafe, sanitation is poor, or repeated diarrhoea becomes part of a child’s earliest years?
A child can be fed and still struggle to grow.
Pakistan’s water figures make this difficult to ignore. According to the WHO/Unicef Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP, 2025), 91 per cent of Pakistan’s population used at least basic drinking-water services in 2024, but only 45pc used safely managed drinking-water services.
That distinction matters. Safely managed water comes from an improved source that is on the premises, available when needed and free from contamination. A water source may therefore be available without the water necessarily being safe.
This is particularly important during the first 1,000 days of a child’s life. Good food, breastfeeding and maternal nutrition are essential. But so is the environment in which a child is growing. Repeated exposure to contaminated water and poor sanitation can mean repeated illness at precisely the stage when healthy growth matters most.
Yet our response is still organised in separate boxes. Nutrition has its programmes. Health has another set of structures. Water and sanitation are often treated as infrastructure. Social protection and climate sit elsewhere.
Children do not experience those divisions. They experience the water available at home, the food they are given, where they play and how often they fall sick.
Our work in rural Punjab has made this very clear.
Through the Behaviour Change and Capacity Development project, WaterAid Pakistan led a consortium, working with the Punjab Rural Municipal Services Company across 200 villages.
The work began not by assuming that people simply needed more information, but by looking at what they were already doing and why.
How was drinking water stored? When were hands washed? How was food prepared? Where did child and animal faeces go? What made a safer practice easy to adopt, and what made it difficult?
That research informed a Hygiene Behaviour Change Package covering safe water, handwashing, food hygiene, sanitation, breastfeeding, vaccination, menstrual hygiene and household and animal waste. Families were engaged repeatedly through community sessions, practical activities, visual materials, videos and behavioural cues.
Our evaluation covered 1,072 households, alongside focus groups, interviews and household observations. Ninety-eight per cent of surveyed households reported adopting new hygiene-related behaviours, 89pc reported washing their hands with soap at critical times, and 86pc reported safe drinking-water use and storage practices.
These figures do not mean behaviour change is the answer to stunting. Nor does one project offer a solution to a national problem. But they do show why infrastructure and behaviour cannot be treated separately.
There is little point in asking a family to use safe water when safe water is not av­­a­ilable. But installing a water system does not automatically change how water is stored, how hands are washed or how waste is managed.
The approach and communication ma­­terials tested in Punjab now form part of PRMSC’s planned expansion to another 1,800 villages. That is important because Pakistan does not lack pilots. The harder task is getting useful evidence into public systems and taking what works to scale.
The same thinking should shape our nutrition response.
When a programme identifies a child at risk of stunting, safe water and sanitation at home should be part of that picture. When a child is treated for diarrhoea, the conditions they return to matter. And when money is being spent on nutrition, health, water or social protection, those investments should work together.
WASH is not the only answer to malnutrition. Food insecurity, poverty, maternal health and access to healthcare remain central.
But what a child eats is only part of the story.
If we want children to grow well, we also need to pay attention to what they drink and the environment in which they spend their earliest years.
The writer is Country Director, WaterAid Pakistan.

title: The AI paradox
author: none@none.com (Huzaifa bin Muneer)
content:
WE’RE building machines that are smart enough to replace us but not wise enough to save us. That’s the contradiction at the heart of the AI debate, and it’s not hypothetical anymore. In September 2026, Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, resigned and publicly stated that the people building AI actually believe the technology could end humanity by the end of this decade (Axios, Sept 2026). 
His colleague Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s alignment science lead, puts the probability of human extinction in the next 10 years at over 10 per cent. Dario Amodei, who runs Anthropic, went further, warning about a swarm of agents that could take over the internet in six to 12 months if nothing is done (Axios, Sept 2026). The people sounding the alarm are the same ones writing the code.
A question that keeps coming back to me is this: what if AI knows everything? What if AI is integrated in every department, in every field? We don’t know the answers, but the reality may be far more dangerous than our worst nightmares.
We’re introducing AI into every discipline as though it was designed for it, with no thought for the ramifications. People are using AI to automate their jobs. They’re handing personal details over to AI-powered large language models (CVs, email accounts, all sorts of data associated with a fairly standard job application). 
It’s quick. It’s efficient. But when the vulnerability exceeds the productivity, we should be limiting that practice or getting rid of it altogether. 
The people sounding the alarm are the same ones writing the code.
What if we don’t actually know what AI is doing with our data? What if it’s hiding information from us and we can’t see that? Its sheer convenience will blind us to the cost.
The infrastructure powering AI has a similarly troubling story to tell. As of August 2026, there are some 12,000 active data centres in the world, with over 4,500 of them in the United States alone (Data Centre Map, August 2026). Where will that number be in 10 years? 
A June 2026 United Nations University report states that in 2025 the world’s data centres consumed 448 trillion watt-hours of electricity, more than all but 10 countries. 
By 2030, they are expected to account for nearly 3pc of global electricity use, emitting some 400 million metric tonnes of CO2 per year (AP/UN University Report, June 2026). More AI means more data centres. More data centres means more environmental damage. The maths doesn’t lie, and it doesn’t forgive.
For Pakistan (ranked the most vulnerable country to climate change in 2022 by the Germanwatch Climate Risk Index), this is no remote threat. The 2022 floods affected a third of the country, killed over 1,700 people and caused damage exceeding $30 billion (Germanwatch CRI 2025). 
As demand for AI infrastructure grows, so does the pressure on energy systems and the climate, with consequences extending far beyond the countries developing the technology. 
AI can help with flood forecasting and crop monitoring, yes. But if the technology enabling that is developed without proper governance, then those benefits are meaningless. 
So, can we just go back to manual systems? In most cases, no. The World Bank’s October 2026 economic update notes that Pakistan is hamstrung by poor broadband penetration, unreliable electricity and a critical lack of di­­gital skills. Nad­ra’s biometric da­­tabases already run using autom­ated systems that would be impractical to replace manually at na­­tio­­nal scale. 
Going back to all that is not an option. The real issue isn’t whether we need AI, but how we adopt it responsibly without making the very problems we are trying to survive worse.
The issue isn’t AI per se. It’s about planning and execution. If we automate everything, then what do we do by hand? And if that automation becomes uncontrolled, do we even have the option to turn it off? 
AI development is consuming massive amounts of money and energy, often with no proportional return. Nobody has all the answers. All we can do is demand that any new data centre proposal undergo a mandatory environmental impact assessment before approval. 
We can demand that AI governance is treated as seriously as AI innovation. If no humans are left, what is the point of AI or its efficiencies? If the world we live in is no longer liveable, no amount of technological development will make any difference. 
The writer is an AI engineer and researcher.
Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

title: Pakistan’s reforms deficit
author: none@none.com (Tahsin Shah)
content:
PAKISTAN has never suffered from a shortage of civil service reform proposals. It has suffered from a shortage of reforms that survive implementation. 
Since independence, successive governments, commissions and committees have attempted to restructure the administrative machinery inherited from the colonial state. Yet familiar complaints persist: excessive generalism, weak accountability, politicisation, distorted incentives, slow decision-making and a bureaucracy often better equipped to process files than solve complex problems. 
The latest reform package is significant not because Pakistan has rediscovered civil service reform, but because it attempts to address several structural weaknesses simultaneously. It proposes 11 specialised professional cadres, competency-based recruitment, performance-linked remuneration, restructuring of training and human-resource management, and a National Executive Service (NES) under which BS-20 and above positions could be opened to serving officials, academics and private-sector professionals.
Pakistan inherited the powerful, generalist Civil Service of Pakistan from the colonial administrative tradition. The most dramatic restructuring came under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in 1973, when the CSP structure was abolished and occupational groups reorganised. But restructuring did not democratise opportunity within government. 
The devolution reforms introduced under Gen Pervez Musharraf in 2001 represented another major intervention, transferring substantial authority towards elected local governments and altering traditional district administration. But institutional discontinuity and subsequent political changes prevented the system from developing into a durable architecture of local governance. 
Reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process.
This history reveals Pakistan’s recurring problem: reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process. 
The strongest feature of the present package is its recognition that a modern state cannot be managed through transferable generalists. Professional cadres in fields including IT and telecom, energy, climate, engineering, health, education, law, agriculture and science address a genuine administrative weakness. 
Opening senior positions to competition could be still more consequential. It could bring specialists into government who would otherwise never enter conventional public service and allow capable career officers to compete beyond rigid cadre boundaries. But lateral entry carries an equally obvious risk: without credible safeguards, it can become lateral patronage. 
International experience offers principles rather than readymade templates. Pakistan should borrow principles, not blindly transplant institutions. 
Performance-linked remuneration illustrates the challenge. Annual performance agreements for ministries, flowing down to individual officers, could improve accountability. But who determines whether a secretary has performed well? If targets are vague or assessments depend excessively upon political superiors, financial incentives could rew­ard proximity to power rather than performance. 
The ultimate measurement must therefore be governance. Does a business licence take days instead of months? Are teachers and doctors present? Are development projects completed on time? Can citizens obtain public services without intermediaries? Can civil servants make lawful professional decisions without seeking political protection? 
Significantly, the Police Service and Foreign Service would remain outside the proposed NES. There are sound reasons for treating them as specialised career services requiring institutional continuity, accumulated professional experience and service-specific training. Their exclusion from the NES, however, need not mean exclusion from reform. 
For the police, Pakistan does not need to start from scratch. In May 2018, then chief justice Mian Saqib Nisar initiated a Police Reforms Committee bringing together nine retired and seven serving Inspectors General of Police. After extensive deliberations, it produced the two-volume Police Reforms: Way Forward, launched in Jan 2019. 
Building upon the Police Order 2002 and subsequent experience, the exercise addressed some of the most persistent weaknesses of policing: accountability, quality and independence of investigation, complaint redressal, urban policing, alternative dispute resolution, counterterrorism and the legal framework governing the police. It proposed a model police law while recognising the constitutional and administrative realities of Pakistan’s federal system. 
Yet the principal structural problems identified by the committee remain largely unresolved. Its convener, former IGP Afzal Ali Shigri, observed as recently as Feb 2026 that fragmented legal frameworks, weaknesses in investigation and uneven accountability mechanisms continue to impede reform. 
The 2019 police reform report thus stands as a telling case study of Pakistan’s persistent gap between designing reform and implementing it. 
The exclusion of the Police Service from the NES presents an opportunity rather than necessarily a deficiency. Instead of forcing policing into an administrative model designed for civilian mi­­nistries, the government can revive Police Reforms: Way Forward, update it and implement its still-relevant recommendations. The Foreign Service can similarly retain its distinctive professional structure while pursuing the broader reform principles of merit, specialisation, transparent advancement and measurable performance. 
The government proposes an ambitious implementation timetable for the new civil-service package. Speed can create momentum, but changing regulations is easier than changing administrative culture. 
No examination reform can compensate for arbitrary postings. No specialised cadre can flourish if expertise is subordinated to connections. No performance contract creates accountability if influence protects poor performance. And no reform report, however professionally drafted, improves governance while it remains on a shelf. 
Pakistan has spent decades reforming bureaucracy on paper. The real reform is to build institutions where competence matters more than cadre, performance more than seniority, expertise more than connections and public service more than institutional privilege. 
The writer is a former Inspector General of Police and DG FIA.
Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

title: Quintessential capitalism
author: none@none.com (Zafar Masud)
content:
FEW companies are hailed as proof of free-market genius more than Tesla. Yet, at every turn that mattered, it stood on public capital. In 2010 it borrowed $465m from a US federal programme open to every carmaker building cleaner vehicles, in a country where transport is now the largest source of greenhouse gases. It paid the Treasury’s own cost, roughly one to 3.4 per cent, with principal deferred until production began. One of the smallest borrowers, it became the star, repaying with interest nine years early. Regulatory credits, earned by beating emission rules and bought by those that fall short, then carried it into profit.
Pakistan asks its banks to do alone what no quintessential capitalist economy asks of its own: lend to priority sectors without the state sharing the risk and the price. This is not a lesson taken from state-led economies such as China, where public support is part of the model. It comes from the market economies themselves, which do it openly and without apology. Tesla is not their exception; it is their method.
Look at where they aim interest subsidies, and how deep. Farming comes first: America lends beginning farmers money to buy land at under 2pc and caps their operating microloans at 5pc, while Canada pays the interest on the first C$250,000 of each grower’s cash advance. Housing is next: France gives first-time buyers zero-interest loans and compensates banks through tax credits. Then enterprise: Britain lends start-ups unsecured at a fixed 6pc, with mentoring, and its firms outlive their peers; Germany’s KfW cheapens founders’ loans and absorbs four-fifths of any loss so local banks will lend.
In every case, the taxpayer took the first risk and part of the financing cost, at the stage private finance would not, and demanded performance in return. And the subsidy went to the borrower, the priority-sector player, not the lender: the bank is paid only the market interest the borrower is spared.
Subsidies have built giants, and an emerging economy needs them more, not less.
That is the global norm. Why, then, is Pakistan so averse to it? Here, subsidy for producers is treated as a dirty word, subsidised credit is misread as a benefit to banks, and lenders are blamed for holding back from risks their peers abroad never shoulder unaided. Asking them to match the world’s lending without the world’s toolkit is neither fair nor realistic.
The money exists; its direction is the problem. This year’s federal budget allocates Rs838bn to the Benazir Income Support Programme, up by a sixth, and almost as much to the power sector; provincial budgets add their own spending on wheat, fertiliser and household relief. Little of it is designed to make the poor bankable.
BISP is indispensable. Reaching some 10 million families through a national registry and digital payments, it is one of the country’s institutional achievements, and that safety net must stay. But a stipend, by its nature, protects rather than transforms. A net that never becomes a springboard keeps the poor safe, but poor.
BISP must now be balanced with wealth creation at the lower strata of society, so that families able to work have a path from support to enterprise. Wealth, like subsidy, is not a bad word. It can be created at every level, including the bottom, and it is what keeps incomes rising sustainably. The cliché about wealth must go, just like subsidies.
So add a ramp without lowering the floor: dedicate a tenth of BISP’s allocation to an enterprise window within the programme; that is smaller than this year’s increase, so no family need receive less than last year.
Run it as the world does. Target precisely: older people, persons with disabilities and households with no working member keep their full stipend; working-age households, starting with the women BISP serves, get concessional credit for livestock, horticulture, cottage industry, solar trades and digital work. Price it for the borrower: the first loan interest-free and repeat loans at no more than 5pc, the state paying the difference. Pay for delivery: lenders earn the subsidy only for verified results, and every loan comes with training and a mentor. Build the exit: the stipend tapers only once the business stands, and the subsidy steps down with each cycle.
Even at today’s rates, that tenth could carry some Rs400bn of lending: over a million small businesses. Audit it independently after three years; scale it only if it works.
Two objections deserve answers. Credit alone, global trials show, raises poor families’ incomes only modestly; what lifts them for good is capital paired with training and continued support while the business finds its feet, which is this design. Nor does the window raid BISP: it is paid for from the programme’s growth and serves the same households.
It is time to retire the reflex that subsidies never create wealth or welfare. Bad design is bad; subsidy is not, if it pays for the initial risk rather than permanent inefficiency. Subsidies have built giants, and an emerging economy needs them more, not less.
Washington’s decisive bet on Tesla was not a stipend but a loan, tied to milestones. Pakistan’s Teslas are smaller — a woman’s dairy herd, a tailor’s workshop, a graduate’s laptop — but they deserve the same deal: capital to start, conditions to keep, and a way out. Then the cycle begins again with the next borrower. That is routine in every quintessential capitalist economy, and it should be in Pakistan too.
The writer is a development-focused and impact-oriented banker.
Published in Dawn, October 30th, 2026
